section: Caching Tiers: Keeping Hot Data in Memory
title: One home screen, dozens of reads: why every giant adds caches
body: Picture a global app with 1 billion users. A single home-screen load might read a profile, 50 friend names, 20 post counters and some settings. Multiply that by hundreds of millions of daily users and the database would face an enormous read rate. Durable stores are slow and expensive per read compared to memory, so almost every large company answers the same way: put caches in front of storage. Caches keep hot data in memory so most reads never reach the database at all.
deeper: This chapter follows a clear arc. First it explains why caches exist and the four classic patterns for wiring them up. Then it tackles the hard part: keeping the cache correct when the source of truth changes, which is where most caching bugs live. Next come the special problems that only appear at scale: thundering herds (thousands of simultaneous misses), hot keys (one key getting a huge share of traffic), and cold caches (an empty cache suddenly facing full load). The middle of the chapter walks through real systems: Meta's memcache deployment and its CacheLib library, Netflix's EVCache, Twitter/X's Twemcache and Pelikan, and Uber's CacheFront. It then covers Redis and Valkey, flash-backed caches, and the CDN as the outermost cache layer. It ends with sizing and hit-ratio math and a catalogue of failure modes. The running example (1 billion users, a heavy home screen) returns in the sizing section to show how small changes in hit ratio translate into large changes in database load.

quiz.q: Why is putting a cache in front of storage the near-universal answer to read-heavy apps?
quiz.a: Memory reads are far faster and cheaper per read than durable storage, so serving repeated reads from memory spares the database an otherwise enormous read rate.

title: A cache is a copy you are allowed to lose
body: A cache is a fast, smaller copy of data whose real home, the source of truth, lives somewhere slower. The defining property: a cache can lose data and the system is still correct, because anything missing can be read again from the source. That one fact shapes every design choice in caching. The price is real though: another system to operate, extra memory, and above all stale data, because the source of truth and the cache can disagree. Most caching bugs live in that gap.
deeper:
Because the cache is disposable, you can make aggressive choices you would never make for a database. You can drop requests under load and treat them as misses, restart nodes freely, evict data whenever memory runs short, and keep only one copy of an item. Meta, for example, sends gets over UDP and simply treats dropped packets as misses. None of that would be acceptable for data of record.

The flip side is that disposability only covers correctness, not capacity. An empty cache still gives correct answers, but the database may not survive serving all of them, which is why later sections treat big caches as load-bearing. And the disagreement between cache and source is the core engineering problem: every write to the source of truth creates a window in which the cache may hold an old value. The chapter's invalidation section, with its stale-set, replication-lag and lost-invalidation races, is entirely about shrinking and bounding that window. When you evaluate any caching design, ask two separate questions: what happens to correctness if the cache is lost, and what happens to load.

quiz.q: Why can a cache drop data without making the system incorrect, and what problem does that not solve?
quiz.a: The source of truth still has the data, so misses just re-read it. It does not solve staleness (cache and source disagreeing) or the load spike when the cache is empty.

title: Latency and offload: a cache server can replace tens of DBs
body: Caches deliver latency and offload. Reading from memory on a nearby server takes well under a millisecond, while a database read that touches disk and replicas can take several milliseconds, and much more at the tail. Offload means every cache hit is a request the database never serves. Meta's CacheLib paper (2020) notes that a single caching server can replace tens of backend database servers, thanks to about 20 times higher throughput and hit ratios above 80 percent.
deeper:
The two benefits multiply. Higher throughput per server means one cache box handles what many database boxes would; a high hit ratio means only a small fraction of requests fall through. With 20 times the throughput and more than 80 percent of reads absorbed, the database fleet needed for the remaining misses shrinks dramatically.

The tail point matters for user-facing pages. A page load at Meta can fetch hundreds of keys, so overall page latency is set by the slowest of many reads. A database read that is usually a few milliseconds but occasionally much slower will regularly show up in some page's critical path. Serving most of those reads from memory in well under a millisecond compresses the tail as well as the median. Uber's CacheFront results illustrate this: after adding an integrated Redis cache it reported p75 latency down 75 percent and p99.9 latency down more than 67 percent (2024).

The catch, developed later in the chapter, is that offload becomes a dependency: if the database fleet is sized for only the miss traffic, losing the cache means losing the service.

quiz.q: Why do caches help tail latency and not just average latency?
quiz.a: Pages fan out to many reads and wait for the slowest. Memory reads are consistently sub-millisecond, while database reads can spike at the tail, so caching removes most slow reads from the critical path.

title: Uber: 3,000 Redis cores instead of 60,000 database cores
body: Caches also save money. Serving a read from memory needs far less CPU than a database read, which must parse SQL, take locks and read B-tree pages. The chapter's standout example: Uber reported one use case serving 6 million reads per second with about 3,000 Redis cores, instead of an estimated 60,000 database cores (2024). That is roughly a twentyfold reduction in compute for the same read traffic, simply by answering repeated reads from a key-value lookup in memory.
deeper:
The CPU gap comes from how much work each path does. A database read goes through query parsing and planning, concurrency control (locks or equivalent), and page-oriented storage structures like B-trees, possibly with disk I/O. A cache read is essentially a hash lookup on a key and a memory copy of the value. Even when the database has the data in its own buffer pool, it still pays the parsing and locking overhead on every request.

The Uber number comes from CacheFront, its cache integrated into the Docstore query engine, which overall serves over 40 million reads per second. The comparison is an estimate for one use case, but it shows why caching is often a cost decision rather than only a latency decision: at millions of reads per second, the database cores you avoid buying dominate the cost of running the cache fleet.

The costs on the other side of the ledger are an extra system to operate, extra memory, and the correctness risk of stale data. Those costs are why the rest of the chapter focuses on invalidation and failure handling.

quiz.q: Why does a cache hit need so much less CPU than a database read, even if the database has the row in memory?
quiz.a: The database still parses SQL, takes locks and walks B-tree pages per request; a cache does a key lookup and returns bytes.

title: Senior lens: could the database survive if the cache were empty?
body: A cache starts as a performance tool and quietly becomes a capacity dependency. Once the database is sized only for the traffic that misses the cache, losing the cache means losing the database. The senior staff question for every design review: if this cache were empty right now, could the database survive the load? If the answer is no, the cache is load-bearing, and its failure and warmup paths must be designed as carefully as the database itself.
deeper:
Caches drift into this state gradually. A team adds a cache to cut latency, the hit ratio climbs, the database looks underused, and someone right-sizes the database fleet to save money. Now the database can only handle the miss traffic. The sizing section makes the math concrete: with 2 million reads per second and a database limit of 100,000, a hit ratio of 95 percent already puts the database at its limit, and anything lower is an outage.

Designing the failure path means planning for mass restarts, deploys, node failures and regional failover. The chapter shows how big companies do this: Meta's Gutter pool absorbs failed servers' traffic and Cold Cluster Warmup fills new clusters from warm peers, CacheLib offers warm restarts, Netflix EVCache and Uber CacheFront replicate caches across regions so failover lands on warm caches. The DynamoDB paper takes a different angle, deliberately sending constant refresh traffic to its metadata fleet so it never depends on a hit ratio. Alternatives include admission control and load shedding in front of the database.

quiz.q: What makes a cache 'load-bearing', and what must you then design carefully?
quiz.a: The database cannot survive the full read load if the cache is empty. You must design the cache's failure, restart and warmup paths as carefully as the database.

title: Look-aside caching: the app checks, misses, fills, and deletes
body: In look-aside (cache-aside) caching, the application owns all the logic. On a read it checks the cache; on a miss it reads the database and puts the value into the cache. On a write it writes the database, then deletes the cache entry rather than updating it. The next reader refills it. Meta calls its memcache usage a demand-filled look-aside cache. This is the dominant pattern at big-tech scale and the model behind most web caches.
deeper:
Walk through a concrete flow. The app calls get(user:42) on the cache and gets a miss. It runs SELECT for profile 42 against the database, receives the row, and calls set(user:42, row). Later a write happens: the app runs UPDATE profile 42 against the database, gets ok, and then calls delete(user:42). The cache is now empty for that key until the next reader fills it.

The strengths: the database remains the source of truth, so there is no data-loss risk if the cache dies, and the cache only holds data that someone actually read. The weaknesses: every service must implement the logic correctly, and the gap between reading the database and filling the cache opens races. A reader can fill an old value after a writer's delete (the stale set), or fill from a lagging replica. So look-aside with delete-on-write is only eventually consistent. The chapter's fixes, including leases, versioned values, commit-log invalidation and TTLs, all exist to patch those races. Uber's CacheFront moves this same logic into the database query engine so teams cannot forget the delete.

quiz.q: In look-aside caching, who fills the cache, and what does a write do to the cache?
quiz.a: The application fills it after a miss by reading the database. A write goes to the database first, then the application deletes the cache key.

title: Why delete on write instead of updating the cache
body: On a write, look-aside caches delete the cached entry instead of writing the new value into it. Two reasons. First, deletes are idempotent: doing one twice is harmless. Second, updating invites a race where two writers update the cache in the opposite order from the database, leaving the cache permanently holding the older value. With delete, there is nothing to reorder: the entry is simply gone, and the next reader refills it with whatever the database currently holds.
deeper:
Consider two writers, A and B, changing the same row. A writes value 1 to the database, then B writes value 2, so the database ends at 2. If each writer then sets its own value into the cache, network or scheduling delays can deliver B's set first and A's set second. The cache now says 1 while the database says 2, and nothing will correct it until the entry expires or is written again.

With delete-on-write, both writers send delete. Order does not matter, and a duplicated or retried delete does no harm, which also makes deletes easy to retry and to broadcast from a log. The next reader misses and reads 2 from the database.

Deleting does not remove every race: a slow reader can still fill an old value after the delete, the stale-set problem that Meta's leases fix. And it has a cost: every write causes at least one future miss. For most read-heavy workloads that is a good trade, which is why the chapter lists it as a key takeaway: look-aside with delete-on-write is the dominant pattern at scale.

quiz.q: Why does Meta delete cache entries on write instead of updating them?
quiz.a: Deletes are idempotent and avoid races where concurrent updates reach the cache in a different order than the database. The next reader refills with the current value.

title: Read-through: let the cache talk to the database
body: In a read-through cache, the cache itself loads from the database on a miss. The application only ever talks to the cache, never directly to the database for reads. This centralizes the miss-handling logic in one place instead of scattering it across every service, but it means the cache must know how to query the database. Staleness and data-loss characteristics are the same as look-aside. Uber's CacheFront is an example of this kind of integrated cache.
deeper:
The trade-off between look-aside and read-through is about where logic lives. In look-aside, each application team writes the check, miss, read, fill sequence and the delete on write, and each team can get it subtly wrong. In read-through, one component owns that logic, which makes it easier to add protections once for everyone: stale-fill guards, negative caching, invalidation from a log.

The cost is coupling. A generic key-value cache like memcached knows nothing about SQL schemas; to be read-through it needs to understand how a key maps to a query. That is why read-through tends to show up as a feature of a database platform rather than a standalone cache. Uber's CacheFront sits inside Docstore's query engine: the engine checks Redis, returns cached rows, fetches the rest from storage and fills Redis asynchronously. The chapter's comparison table rates read-through the same as look-aside for write cost (database write plus delete), staleness risk and data-loss risk (none, since the database is still truth).

quiz.q: What does read-through gain over look-aside, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Miss handling lives in one place so apps only talk to the cache, but the cache must know how to query the database, coupling it to the data model.

title: Write-through: always fresh, but every write pays twice
body: In write-through caching, writes go to the cache, and the cache synchronously writes to the database before acknowledging. The cache is therefore always fresh for keys that were written, and nothing is lost if the cache fails because the database already has the write. The downsides: every write pays both latencies, the cache and the database, and you end up caching data that may never be read. It suits small, hot data like configuration and sessions.
deeper:
Write-through fixes one specific staleness problem: after a write, readers of that key see the new value immediately from the cache, with no window where an old value lingers. The chapter's comparison table marks its staleness risk as low for written keys and its data-loss risk as none.

But it has two costs that make it a poor default at scale. First, write latency is the sum of the cache write and the database write, since the acknowledgment waits for both. Second, every written key lands in cache memory whether or not anyone will read it, which wastes memory on write-heavy, read-rarely data and can evict hot keys. Keys that were never written through (for example, rows changed by some other path) can still be stale.

That is why the typical use is small, hot data: configuration values read constantly and written rarely, and user sessions. For large datasets with many writes, look-aside with delete-on-write avoids paying for caching unread data.

quiz.q: Why is write-through a poor fit for large write-heavy datasets?
quiz.a: Every write pays cache plus database latency, and every written key occupies cache memory even if never read, wasting memory and possibly evicting hot data.

title: Write-back: fastest writes, but a dead node loses data
body: In write-back (write-behind) caching, writes go to the cache and are acknowledged immediately. The cache writes to the database later, in batches. This gives the fastest writes of any pattern, but if the cache node dies before flushing, those writes are lost. At big-tech scale, write-back is used for counters and metrics that can tolerate a small loss, never for user data of record, because the cache briefly becomes the only holder of the data.
deeper:
Write-back breaks the rule that makes caches safe: normally a cache can lose anything because the source of truth has it. Between acknowledgment and flush, the cache is the source of truth, so a crash, a restart or an eviction bug destroys acknowledged writes.

The benefit is throughput. Batching lets many increments to the same counter collapse into a single database write, and the client never waits for the database. For a like counter or a metrics pipeline, losing a few seconds of increments during a rare node failure is an acceptable price for absorbing a huge write rate cheaply. The comparison table lists its write cost as lowest, staleness as low, and data-loss risk as yes, on cache failure, with typical uses of counters, metrics and buffers.

The decision test from the chapter's quiz: write-back is acceptable only when losing the most recent writes on a cache failure is acceptable, such as approximate counters or metrics, and never for data of record like a user's profile or a payment.

quiz.q: When is write-back caching acceptable?
quiz.a: When losing the most recent writes on a cache failure is acceptable, such as approximate counters or metrics, and never for data of record.

title: Four cache patterns side by side
body: The four patterns differ in who fills the cache and when it is updated. Look-aside: the application fills on a miss; write cost is a database write plus delete; used by most web caches and memcache at Meta. Read-through: the cache fills on a miss; same costs; used in integrated caches like Uber CacheFront. Write-through: the cache writes the database synchronously; higher write cost; used for small hot configs and sessions. Write-back: the cache flushes later; lowest write cost; used for counters, metrics and buffers.
deeper:
The comparison table adds two more columns that decide most choices. Staleness risk: look-aside and read-through both suffer races between a fill and a delete; write-through has low staleness for written keys; write-back is low too since the cache holds the newest value. Data-loss risk: look-aside, read-through and write-through all have none, because the database remains the truth. Only write-back risks loss, on cache failure.

A useful way to read the table: moving from look-aside toward write-back trades durability for write speed, and moving from look-aside toward read-through trades application flexibility for centralized correctness. At big-tech scale the common landing point is look-aside or read-through with delete-on-write for data of record, plus invalidation from the database commit log and a TTL as safety net, while write-back is reserved for data that can tolerate small loss. Write-through appears where a small set of keys must be fresh immediately after writes and write latency is acceptable.

quiz.q: Which of the four cache patterns is the only one with data-loss risk, and why?
quiz.a: Write-back, because writes are acknowledged before reaching the database, so a cache node dying before flushing loses them.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: The stale set: how a paused reader poisons the cache
body: Phil Karlton's famous joke says the two hard things in computer science are cache invalidation and naming things. The first race shows why. Reader A misses, reads the old value from the database, then pauses, perhaps for a garbage-collection pause. Writer B updates the database and deletes the cache key. Reader A wakes up and sets the old value into the cache. Now the cache holds stale data with no expiry in sight. Meta's memcache paper calls this a stale set.
deeper:
The stale set is nasty because every participant did the right thing. The reader followed look-aside exactly, and the writer wrote the database and then deleted the key. The problem is ordering: the writer's delete landed in the gap between the reader's database read and its cache fill, so the delete removed nothing and the fill resurrected old data. Delete-on-write cannot help, because the delete already happened.

Without further protection, the stale value lives until something else evicts it or a TTL expires it. If no TTL is set, it can live effectively forever. That is why the chapter insists on always setting a TTL even when you also invalidate.

The specific fixes come later. Meta's leases give each miss a token that a later delete invalidates, so the delayed set is rejected. Uber's CacheFront uses versioning: Lua scripts in Redis compare timestamps so a late fill cannot overwrite fresher data. Both fixes work by letting the cache detect that the fill is older than something that already happened.

quiz.q: Describe the stale-set race in look-aside caching.
quiz.a: A reader misses and reads the old value, then stalls. A writer updates the database and deletes the key. The reader then fills the cache with the old value, which stays stale.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: Replication lag: the delete beats the replica
body: The second invalidation race comes from database replication. The application writes to the primary database in one region and deletes the cache key. A reader in another region then misses and reads from its local replica, which has not yet received the write. It fills the cache with the old value. The invalidation was correct and timely, but the data source used to refill the cache was itself stale, so the cache ends up stale again right after being cleaned.
deeper:
This race appears whenever reads go to asynchronous replicas while writes go to a primary, which is the normal setup for multi-region systems. At Meta, one region holds the primary databases and other regions hold replicas.

Two industry techniques address it. The first is to tie invalidation to replication itself: Meta's McSqueal invalidations flow with MySQL replication, so a region's cache deletes arrive alongside the data change rather than racing ahead of it. The second is Meta's remote markers. When a web server in a non-primary region writes, it sets a marker in the regional cache, writes to the primary region's database, and deletes the local key. A later reader that sees the marker knows the local replica may be behind and reads from the primary region instead. This protects read-after-write for users outside the primary region.

Versioning also helps when a later fill carries a newer version: an older value cannot overwrite a newer cached one.

quiz.q: Why can deleting a cache key right after a write still lead to a stale cache in a multi-region setup?
quiz.a: A reader in another region can miss and refill from a local replica that has not yet received the write, putting the old value back.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: Lost invalidations: the delete that never arrives
body: The third race is the simplest: the invalidation never happens. The application writes the database but crashes before sending the delete to the cache. Or the delete is sent, but over a network that drops it. Either way the database holds the new value while the cache keeps serving the old one, and nothing in the application will ever retry. Any design that relies on application code to remember and successfully deliver every delete will eventually leak stale entries.
deeper:
This race is why big companies moved invalidation out of application code and into the database's commit log. Meta runs McSqueal on every database: it reads committed SQL statements, extracts the cache keys to invalidate, and broadcasts deletes. Uber's CacheFront uses Flux, which tails the MySQL binlog. Because the log is durable and ordered, an invalidation cannot be lost when an app server crashes, and it can be replayed after a failure. The write is committed if and only if it is in the log, so every committed write eventually produces its delete.

Even then, a TTL remains the backstop for anything that slips through: a bug in key extraction, a code path that writes without going through the normal flow, or an operational mishap. The chapter's failure-mode list states it bluntly: a missed invalidation with no TTL lives forever.

The common mistake box ties it together: invalidating on write does not make a cache consistent unless these races are handled.

quiz.q: Why is invalidating from the database commit log more reliable than sending deletes from application code?
quiz.a: The log is durable and ordered, so invalidations survive app crashes and dropped messages and can be replayed; application-sent deletes can simply be lost.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: Always set a TTL: it bounds staleness you didn't prevent
body: TTL (time to live) makes every cache entry expire after some fixed time. A TTL does not prevent staleness; a stale value still serves until it expires. What it does is bound staleness: no matter which race or bug left an entry wrong, it cannot stay wrong longer than the TTL. The chapter's rule is to always set a TTL, even if you also invalidate on write or from a log. It is the safety net for bugs.
deeper:
Think of invalidation and TTL as two layers with different jobs. Invalidation, ideally from the commit log, keeps the cache fresh in the normal case, within seconds of a write. TTL guarantees an upper bound when invalidation fails: a stale set, a lost delete, a replication-lag refill, or a bug that writes the database through a path nobody hooked up.

Without a TTL, the failure mode is severe. The chapter's failure list notes that a missed invalidation with no TTL lives forever, and a stale set can leave data stale with no expiry in sight.

TTL choice has knock-on effects. Short TTLs reduce staleness but increase misses and database load. And many keys written together with the same TTL will expire together, causing a stampede; the chapter's fix is jittered TTLs, such as 1 hour plus or minus 10 minutes. Local in-process caches for hot keys use very short TTLs, measured in seconds, precisely because they receive no invalidations. Gutter pool entries at Meta also expire quickly.

quiz.q: If you already invalidate caches from the commit log, why still set a TTL?
quiz.a: TTL bounds how long any stale entry can survive when invalidation fails through bugs, races or unhooked write paths. It is the safety net, not the primary mechanism.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: McSqueal and Flux: invalidation from the commit log
body: Big companies drive invalidation from the database's commit log instead of application code. Meta runs a daemon called McSqueal on every database: it reads committed SQL statements, extracts the cache keys to invalidate, and broadcasts deletes to all frontend clusters in the region. Uber's CacheFront does the same with Flux, which tails the MySQL binlog. Because the log is durable and ordered, invalidations cannot be lost when an app server crashes, and they can be replayed.
deeper:
The data flow: web servers send SQL writes to the MySQL primary. The primary records them in its commit log or binlog. An invalidation daemon (McSqueal or Flux) reads that log and sends batched deletes to a cache router in each cluster, such as mcrouter, which forwards them to the cache servers. Meanwhile web servers keep doing get, and fill on miss, against the caches.

This decouples correctness from application code. A team that adds a new write path does not need to remember which keys to delete, as long as the daemon can derive keys from the committed change. At Meta, McSqueal invalidations also flow with MySQL replication to other regions, so deletes in a replica region follow the data that caused them.

At Uber, Flux invalidates or updates Redis within seconds, and the write path also invalidates directly so the writer gets fresh reads sooner. CacheFront's own design adds Lua timestamp checks, since log-driven invalidation alone does not stop a late fill from resurrecting old data.

quiz.q: How does McSqueal know which cache keys to delete?
quiz.a: It reads committed SQL statements from the database's log, extracts the affected cache keys, and broadcasts deletes to the region's frontend clusters.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: Versioned values: never let old data overwrite new
body: Versioning stores a version number or timestamp with each cached value and refuses to overwrite a newer value with an older one. This directly defends against late fills, where a slow reader tries to put stale data into the cache after fresher data is already there. Uber's CacheFront implements this with Lua scripts running inside Redis that compare row timestamps, so a late fill cannot overwrite fresher data. The comparison happens atomically in the cache, not in the application.
deeper:
Why run the check inside Redis with a Lua script? Because a compare-then-set done from the application would have its own race: two clients could each read the current version, each decide theirs is newer, and both write. A script executes atomically on the Redis server, so the compare and the write happen as one step.

Versioning complements the other techniques. Log-driven invalidation keeps the cache fresh and guarantees deletes are not lost. TTL bounds anything that slips through. Versioning handles the ordering problem: whenever two writes to the cache race, the newer data wins regardless of arrival order. Meta's leases solve a similar problem differently, by invalidating a filler's token when a delete arrives.

The chapter also recommends versioned values as one way to give read-your-writes to a feature that needs it: a client that knows the version it just wrote can detect an older cached value. The alternative is routing that user's reads to the database for a short time after they write.

quiz.q: Why does CacheFront compare timestamps inside Redis with Lua scripts rather than in application code?
quiz.a: The script runs atomically on the server, so the compare and the write cannot interleave with another client's fill, preventing a late fill from overwriting fresher data.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: Remote markers: read-after-write for far-away users
body: Remote markers protect read-after-write for users outside the primary region. When a Meta web server in a non-primary region writes, it first sets a marker in the regional cache, then writes to the primary region's database, then deletes the local cache key. A later reader that sees the marker knows the local replica may not have the write yet, so it reads from the primary region instead of the lagging local replica. Without the marker, it would refill from stale data.
deeper:
The problem being solved is the replication-lag race. In Meta's design one region holds the primary databases and others hold replicas. A user in a replica region who updates their profile and immediately reloads would otherwise miss the cache, read the local replica, get the old profile and cache it again. Users notice when their own change seems to vanish.

The marker is a small, cheap signal stored in the fast cache layer. It turns a region-wide consistency problem into a per-key decision: most reads keep using the local replica, and only keys with a recent remote write pay the cost of a cross-region read. That extra latency is limited to the short window when it matters.

This idea connects to the chapter's advice for read-your-writes in general: route a user's reads to the database (or primary) for a short time after they write, or use versioned values. Remote markers are one production implementation of that routing.

quiz.q: What problem do Meta's remote markers solve, and how?
quiz.a: They prevent a reader in a replica region from refilling the cache from a lagging replica after a recent write; seeing the marker, the reader goes to the primary region.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: Meta: only 4% of invalidations actually hit cached data
body: Meta found that most invalidations delete nothing: only 4 percent of deletes hit data that was actually cached. Yet every write still produced deletes, and sending them directly from every database to every cache server created packet rates that were too high. The fix was batching. McSqueal batches deletes and sends them to a few mcrouter servers per cluster, which fan them out to the cache servers. Batching improved the median number of deletes per packet by 18 times.
deeper:
Why do so few deletes hit anything? A cache holds only what was recently read, and a write invalidates every key that might depend on it, whether or not that key is currently cached. With log-driven invalidation you cannot cheaply know which keys are present, so you send deletes for all of them and most are no-ops. Deletes being idempotent makes this safe.

The cost is network overhead, not correctness. With many databases and many cache servers, an all-to-all delete stream means a huge number of small packets. Routing through a few mcrouter servers per cluster changes the topology: databases talk to a handful of routers, which pack many deletes per packet and fan them out locally. The 18 times improvement in median deletes per packet is what made commit-log invalidation practical at Meta's scale.

The broader lesson is that at scale, the invalidation path itself is a traffic source you must engineer, not a free side effect of writes.

quiz.q: Why did Meta route invalidations through a few mcrouter servers per cluster instead of sending them directly?
quiz.a: Direct all-to-all deletes created too many packets, and most deleted nothing. Batching through a few routers packed deletes together, improving median deletes per packet by 18 times.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
title: Common mistake: 'we invalidate on write, so we're consistent'
body: A common mistake is believing that invalidating on write makes the cache consistent. It does not, unless the stale-set, replication-lag and lost-invalidation races are handled. Look-aside caching with delete-on-write is eventually consistent: the cache converges to the database's value, but a reader can briefly or even lastingly see old data. If a feature needs read-your-writes, route that user's reads to the database for a short time after they write, or use versioned values.
deeper:
The mistake usually shows up as a bug report like 'I changed my name and the old one came back'. The team checks the code, sees the delete right after the write, and concludes the cache must be fine. But the delete only closes one gap. A reader that started before the write can fill old data after the delete. A reader in another region can refill from a lagging replica. A crash between write and delete can skip the invalidation entirely.

Decide explicitly which guarantee each feature needs. Most reads, like counts of friends or post counters, tolerate a few seconds of staleness. Some interactions, like a user seeing their own just-saved edit, need read-your-writes. For those, the chapter suggests short-term routing to the database after a write, which Meta implements across regions with remote markers, or versioned values so an older cached value can be recognized. Add leases or timestamp checks to reject stale fills, a commit-log invalidator to stop lost deletes, and a TTL to bound the rest.

quiz.q: What consistency does look-aside with delete-on-write give, and how can a feature get read-your-writes?
quiz.a: Eventual consistency. For read-your-writes, route the user's reads to the database for a short time after they write, or use versioned values.

title: Thundering herds: one expired key, thousands of DB hits
body: A thundering herd, also called a cache stampede, happens when a popular key disappears and thousands of requests miss at the same moment. The key might vanish through expiry, invalidation, eviction or a cache restart. All those requests go to the database for the same row. The database slows down, requests time out, clients retry, and the load gets worse rather than better. One missing key can turn a healthy database into an overloaded one in seconds.
deeper:
The herd is a feedback loop. The first wave of misses adds load; the added load raises database latency; higher latency causes timeouts; timeouts cause retries; retries add more load. Because each missing request would also try to fill the cache, the cache stays empty until one of them completes, prolonging the herd.

Popular keys are the dangerous ones precisely because they are popular: the more requests per second a key receives, the more requests pile up during the few milliseconds it takes to refill it. And databases are provisioned for peak load, so herd spikes directly drive hardware cost.

The chapter presents several defenses. Meta's leases, which rate-limit refills to one client per key at a time. Request coalescing, or single-flight, merging concurrent misses in one process or proxy. Jittered TTLs so keys written together do not expire together. Early probabilistic refresh of hot keys before they expire. And serving stale data on error when the database is overloaded. Failure-mode mitigations like capped retries and backoff also stop the retry spiral.

quiz.q: Why does a thundering herd get worse over time instead of resolving itself?
quiz.a: Simultaneous misses slow the database, causing timeouts and client retries that add even more load, while the key stays uncached until a fill completes.

title: Leases kill the stale set with a 64-bit token
body: Meta's leases (2013) fix the stale-set race with one small mechanism. On a miss, memcached gives the client a lease: a 64-bit token tied to that key. The client reads the database and sets the value along with the token. If a delete for that key arrived in the meantime, memcached has already invalidated the token, so the set is rejected. The slow reader holding an old value can no longer overwrite the cache after a writer's delete.
deeper:
Replay the stale-set race with leases. Reader A misses and receives lease token T for key K. A reads the old value from the database, then pauses. Writer B updates the database and sends delete(K). Memcached deletes K and marks token T invalid. Reader A wakes up and tries set(K, old value, T). Memcached sees T is no longer valid and rejects the set. The next reader misses, gets a fresh token, and fills the current value.

The beauty is that the cache itself detects the ordering problem. The application does not need timestamps or versions from the database; the token captures 'nothing has changed since you started your read'. The same mechanism doubles as herd protection, as the next card explains.

Leases also allow returning slightly stale values. Recently deleted items are kept briefly, and a client that can tolerate staleness gets the old value instead of waiting for a fresh fill. Uber's CacheFront solves the same stale-fill problem differently, with timestamp comparisons in Redis Lua scripts.

quiz.q: How do leases prevent the stale-set race?
quiz.a: A miss gets a token; a delete for that key invalidates the token, so a delayed reader's set with the old value is rejected.

title: Leases tame herds: one refill per key every 10 seconds
body: Leases also stop thundering herds. Memcached hands out a lease token for a given key at most once every 10 seconds. Other clients that miss during that window get a wait-and-retry-shortly response instead of going to the database. Usually, by the time they retry, the lease holder has filled the value, so they hit. Meta's paper reports that for keys prone to herds, peak database query rate fell from 17,000 per second to 1,300 per second.
deeper:
Without leases, every client that misses a hot key goes to the database, so a key receiving thousands of requests per second sends thousands of identical queries. With leases, exactly one client per key per 10-second window is allowed to fetch; everyone else waits a moment and reads the freshly filled value from the cache.

The 17,000 to 1,300 drop is at peak, and that is the number that matters: databases are provisioned for peak load, so cutting peak queries is a direct hardware saving, not just a nicer average.

Leases add a further option for staleness-tolerant clients. Recently deleted items are kept briefly, and a client that can accept slightly stale data gets the old value immediately instead of waiting for the lease holder. That trades a little freshness for lower latency during the refill.

The one mechanism therefore solves two problems at once: the token check blocks stale sets, and the rate limit on issuing tokens collapses a herd into a single database read.

quiz.q: How do leases reduce database load during a thundering herd?
quiz.a: Only one client per key gets a lease every 10 seconds to refill it; others are told to wait and retry, and usually hit once the holder fills the value.

title: Single-flight: merge identical misses into one backend call
body: Request coalescing, also called single-flight, is an anti-stampede technique used within one process or proxy. When several concurrent requests miss on the same key, only one backend call is made; the other requests wait for that call and share its result. Instead of a hundred threads querying the database for the same row, one query runs and a hundred callers get the answer. It needs no coordination with the cache server, just local bookkeeping of in-flight keys.
deeper:
Coalescing and leases attack the same herd from different places. Leases coordinate at the cache server, across every client in the fleet. Coalescing works locally, inside a single application process or proxy: it keeps a table of keys with a request already in flight, and new requests for those keys attach to the existing call rather than starting another.

The local scope is both its strength and its limit. It is simple, has no extra round trip, and helps even when the backend is not a cache at all. But with thousands of web servers, each process still sends its own query, so the database can still see one request per process. That is often good enough, and it pairs well with fleet-wide mechanisms like leases.

The chapter's failure-mode diagram lists request coalescing, leases and load shedding together as mitigations for the stage where database latency and timeouts rise after a hit-ratio drop.

quiz.q: What is the limitation of request coalescing compared with leases?
quiz.a: Coalescing only merges misses within one process or proxy, so a large fleet can still send one query per process; leases coordinate across all clients at the cache.

title: Jittered TTLs: don't let a million keys expire at once
body: Jittered TTLs add randomness to expiration times so that many keys written together do not all expire together. For example, instead of a fixed 1-hour TTL, use 1 hour plus or minus 10 minutes. Keys loaded in the same burst, such as after a deploy, a warmup or a batch job, would otherwise hit their expiry at the same instant and send a synchronized wave of misses to the database. Jitter spreads those misses over time.
deeper:
The problem jitter solves is synchronized expiry. Caches are frequently filled in bursts: a cold cache warms up in a few minutes after a restart, or a batch process writes a large set of keys at once. With a fixed TTL, those keys all age out at the same moment one TTL later, and the miss wave repeats every TTL period. It is a thundering herd across many keys instead of on one.

Adding a random offset per key turns that spike into a smooth trickle. In the example, expiries spread across a 20-minute window rather than a single instant, which lowers peak database load, the number that drives provisioning.

Jitter is cheap because it changes only how the TTL is computed. It complements the chapter's other techniques: leases and coalescing handle many requests for one key, jitter handles many keys expiring together, and early refresh keeps the hottest keys from expiring at all while they are in demand.

quiz.q: Why add random jitter to cache TTLs?
quiz.a: Keys written together would otherwise expire together, causing a synchronized wave of misses; jitter spreads expiries out and lowers peak database load.

title: Refresh early, serve stale on error
body: Two more anti-stampede techniques keep a hot key available while its value is renewed. Early, or probabilistic, refresh reloads a hot key in the background shortly before it expires, so readers never see a miss. Serve stale on error means that if the database is overloaded, the cache returns the expired value rather than failing the request. Both trade a little freshness for availability, avoiding the moment where many readers find nothing and rush the database together.
deeper:
Early refresh attacks the root cause of expiry herds: the key disappearing. If a background refresh replaces the value just before its TTL ends, the key never goes missing, so there is no miss wave. Making the refresh probabilistic, so that only some requests near expiry trigger it, avoids every request triggering a refresh at once.

Serve stale on error is a degradation mode. Under normal conditions, expired values are not served. When the database is overloaded, returning a slightly old value keeps the user experience working and, crucially, avoids adding load to a database that is already struggling. This is the same philosophy as Meta's lease feature that keeps recently deleted items briefly and hands them to clients that can tolerate staleness.

Both techniques only make sense for data where brief staleness is acceptable, such as counters, feeds or profiles. For data needing read-your-writes, the chapter's advice is to route reads to the database after a write or use versioned values instead.

quiz.q: How does early probabilistic refresh prevent a stampede on a hot key?
quiz.a: It reloads the key in the background just before expiry, so the key never goes missing and readers never produce a simultaneous miss wave.

title: Hot keys: why sharding the cache can't save you
body: A hot key is a single key that gets a huge share of traffic: a celebrity's profile, a viral post, or a global configuration value. Sharding the cache does not help, because one key lives on one shard; adding servers spreads different keys, not the load of one key. Meta noted that a single key can account for 20 percent of a server's requests. That one server saturates while the rest of the cluster sits comfortably idle.
deeper:
Sharding, whether by consistent hashing or hash slots, maps each key to exactly one owner. That balances load well when traffic spreads over many keys of similar popularity. It fails when traffic concentrates: if one key alone exceeds what a single server can handle, no amount of resharding fixes it, since that key must land somewhere.

Hot keys also make failures worse. If the server holding a hot key dies and its keys are rehashed onto survivors, the hot key can overload the next server, which dies, and so on. Meta's Gutter pool exists partly to prevent this cascade.

The chapter's fixes all change where reads for the key are served rather than how keys are partitioned: replicate hot keys across several cache servers and spread reads, cache the hottest keys locally inside the application with a short TTL, split a key into several copies, and detect hot keys by sampling per-key traffic in the cache proxy so they can be handled before they cause an outage.

quiz.q: Why doesn't adding more cache shards fix a hot key?
quiz.a: Each key maps to exactly one shard, so all traffic for that key still lands on one server no matter how many shards exist.

title: Replicate hot keys: Meta's replicated pools, EVCache per zone
body: The main fix for hot keys is replicating them across several cache servers and spreading reads across the copies. Meta uses replicated pools for this: a set of keys is stored in full on multiple servers, so any replica can answer. Netflix EVCache keeps a full copy of the data in each availability zone and reads from the local zone. Instead of one server absorbing a hot key's entire read rate, the load divides across every copy.
deeper:
Replication trades memory and write work for read capacity. Each extra copy costs memory, and every write or invalidation must reach all copies. That is why it is applied selectively. Meta places workloads with different patterns in separate pools, and keys that benefit from replication go into a replicated pool rather than duplicating everything.

EVCache applies replication more broadly for a different reason. Keeping a full copy per availability zone means reads stay local to the zone, which cuts latency and cross-zone traffic, and a missing item locally (instance failure or eviction) can be read from another zone. Writes go to all zones. Hot keys get spread across zones as a side effect.

The senior staff lens for this section sums up the principle: no partitioning scheme fixes a hot key, so the design must replicate its reads or move them closer to the client. Replication is the first half of that; local in-process caching is the second.

quiz.q: What does replicating a hot key cost, in exchange for spreading its reads?
quiz.a: Extra memory for each copy, and every write or invalidation must update all copies.

title: In-process caches: take the hottest keys off the network
body: For the very hottest keys, the application can keep a local, in-process cache with a short TTL, measured in seconds. Reads for those keys are then answered from the application's own memory without any network call, which takes their load off the network and cache servers entirely. The short TTL is essential: an in-process copy typically receives no invalidations, so the TTL is what bounds how stale it can get. A few seconds of staleness buys huge relief.
deeper:
The math behind local caching is attractive for hot keys. If a global configuration value is read on every request by thousands of web servers, a local copy refreshed every few seconds turns millions of cache reads per second into a handful of refreshes per server. The shared cache server that owns that key stops being a bottleneck.

The cost is consistency. Each process has its own copy, refreshed on its own schedule, so different servers can briefly disagree, and a write takes up to one TTL to become visible everywhere. That is fine for configuration, viral post contents or celebrity profiles where a few seconds of lag is harmless, and not fine where users need read-your-writes.

Local caching also costs application memory, so it is kept to the very hottest keys. To know which keys those are, the chapter recommends detection: sample per-key traffic in the cache proxy and flag keys above a threshold.

quiz.q: Why must an in-process hot-key cache use a very short TTL?
quiz.a: Local copies usually get no invalidations, so the short TTL is the only thing bounding how stale each server's copy can become.

title: Key splitting: store key#1 to key#N and pick one at random
body: Key splitting spreads a hot key by storing several copies under different names, such as key#1 through key#N. Each copy hashes to a different shard, so reads, which pick a random copy, spread across N servers instead of hammering one. The catch is on writes: every write must update or delete all N copies, or readers will see different versions depending on which copy they happen to pick. It is a manual form of replication built on ordinary sharding.
deeper:
Key splitting works with any sharded cache, without special replication support in the cache servers. Because the suffix changes the key, consistent hashing or hash slots will scatter the copies across the cluster, and the read load for the original key divides by roughly N.

The complexity lives in the application. Writers must know the key is split and how many copies exist, and invalidate all of them. If one delete is lost, one copy stays stale and a fraction of readers see old data; a TTL on each copy bounds that. Changing N later requires care so no copy is orphaned.

That is why key splitting is typically reserved for keys known to be hot, found through detection: sampling traffic per key in the cache proxy and alerting on keys above a threshold. The senior staff lens adds the planning angle: ask for the expected top-1 key rate, not just total rate, so you know in advance whether any key will need this treatment.

quiz.q: What must writes do when a hot key is split into key#1 through key#N?
quiz.a: Update or delete all N copies; otherwise readers picking different copies see different versions.

title: Senior lens: ask for the top-1 key rate, not just total QPS
body: Hot keys are the cache version of DynamoDB's single hot item from Chapter 5: no partitioning scheme fixes them. The design must replicate reads or move them closer to the client. So in design reviews, ask for the expected top-1 key rate, not just the total request rate. A system can handle its total load comfortably and still fall over because one key exceeds one server. Pair this with detection: sample traffic per key in the cache proxy and flag keys above a threshold.
deeper:
Total request rate tells you how many servers you need when load is evenly spread. The top-1 key rate tells you whether any single server will be overwhelmed regardless of how many you have. These are different capacity questions, and designs usually only answer the first.

If the top-1 rate is below what one server handles comfortably, ordinary sharding works. If it is close to or above, you need a hot-key strategy up front: replicated pools, per-zone copies, local in-process caching with short TTLs, or key splitting.

Detection covers the keys you did not predict. A viral post or sudden celebrity event creates a hot key nobody planned for. A cache proxy, which already sees every request, can sample per-key traffic and flag keys over a threshold so operators or automation can replicate them. Meta's observation that a single key can reach 20 percent of a server's requests shows the scale of imbalance this can reach. Hot keys also shape failure design: the Gutter pool avoids rehashing a hot key onto a healthy server.

quiz.q: Why should a design review ask for the expected top-1 key rate, not only total request rate?
quiz.a: Total rate sizes the fleet, but one key maps to one server; if that key's rate exceeds a server's capacity, sharding cannot help and replication or local caching is needed.

title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook: the simple server, the huge system
body: The NSDI 2013 paper 'Scaling Memcache at Facebook' describes the largest memcached deployment of its time: billions of requests per second and trillions of items (2013). Memcached itself is a simple in-memory key-value server with just get, set and delete. Meta's contribution is everything around it: routing, networking, pools, failure handling, invalidation and cross-region consistency. Inside a cluster, many memcached servers hold keys spread by consistent hashing, and a page load can fetch hundreds of keys.
deeper:
Because a single page load can fetch hundreds of keys spread across many servers, latency depends on fan-out: the page waits for the slowest of those responses. That shapes many design choices in the paper, from UDP gets to flow control.

The system has three layers. Inside a cluster: memcached servers, consistent hashing, UDP gets, mcrouter for sets and deletes, flow control against incast, pools for different workloads, and a Gutter pool for failures. Across clusters in a region: several frontend clusters share one storage cluster, each frontend cluster with its own full cache, plus a shared regional pool and Cold Cluster Warmup. Across regions: primary databases in one region, replicas elsewhere, with McSqueal invalidations flowing alongside MySQL replication and remote markers protecting read-after-write.

Meta calls this a demand-filled look-aside cache, so all of the look-aside races apply, and the paper introduced leases to address the stale sets and herds. Later, TAO took over many social-graph reads from this layer.

quiz.q: In Meta's memcache design, why does latency depend so much on fan-out?
quiz.a: A page load fetches hundreds of keys across many servers and must wait for the slowest response, so the tail of many parallel requests sets page latency.

title: UDP gets: drop 0.25% of reads, gain 20% lower latency
body: Meta's web servers send memcache gets over UDP directly to the cache servers, avoiding the overhead of TCP connections. At peak, about 0.25 percent of gets are dropped, and clients simply treat those as cache misses. In exchange, UDP gave about 20 percent lower latency than TCP via mcrouter. Only reads use this path; sets and deletes, which must not be silently lost, still go over TCP. It works because a cache is allowed to lose data.
deeper:
This choice is a direct application of the chapter's founding property: a cache can lose data and the system stays correct. A dropped UDP get is indistinguishable from a miss, so correctness is unaffected; the only cost is a small amount of extra database load from those false misses.

There is a subtlety in handling errors. The failure-mode section notes that Meta's clients skip the fill after a UDP get error, to avoid adding load. The request goes to the database for the value, but the client does not write it back into the cache, since the error might indicate congestion and an extra set would make it worse.

Why not UDP for writes? A dropped delete is a lost invalidation, one of the three core consistency races, and a dropped set wastes a database read. So sets and deletes go over TCP through mcrouter, trading a little latency for reliable delivery. At scale, connection overhead matters: with many web servers talking to many cache servers, avoiding per-connection state for the high-volume read path is significant.

quiz.q: Why can Meta safely send memcache gets over UDP but not deletes?
quiz.a: A dropped get just looks like a miss, so correctness holds. A dropped delete is a lost invalidation that leaves stale data, so deletes go over reliable TCP.

title: mcrouter: the proxy that handled 5 billion requests per second
body: At Meta, sets and deletes travel over TCP through mcrouter, a proxy that runs on each web server. mcrouter speaks the memcached protocol, so clients talk to it as if it were memcached. It pools connections to cache servers and routes requests by key prefix, which is how different key families can be sent to different pools. By 2014 mcrouter handled close to 5 billion requests per second at peak. It also relays McSqueal's batched invalidations inside clusters.
deeper:
Running mcrouter locally on each web server gives two big wins. Connection pooling: instead of each application thread opening connections to every cache server, mcrouter maintains shared connections, cutting connection counts and overhead. Routing by key prefix: the key's prefix decides which pool it belongs to, so a low-value, high-churn key family can live in its own pool and not evict valuable keys.

Because mcrouter speaks the memcached protocol, applications need no special client library; they just send memcached commands. That makes it easy to add routing policies, such as sending a failed server's traffic to the Gutter pool, without changing application code.

mcrouter also plays a role in invalidation. McSqueal does not send deletes directly to every cache server; it sends batched deletes to a few mcrouter servers per cluster, which fan them out. Batching through this layer improved median deletes per packet by 18 times. The chapter's invalidation diagram shows the same pattern generically: a cache router per cluster receiving batched deletes from the invalidation daemon.

quiz.q: Why does Meta route cache traffic by key prefix in mcrouter?
quiz.a: The prefix identifies the key family, letting mcrouter send different workloads to separate pools so, for example, high-churn low-value keys do not evict valuable ones.

title: Incast: when too many answers arrive at once
body: Incast congestion happens when many responses arrive at one client at the same time and overflow network switch buffers, causing packet loss and retransmission delays. Meta's page loads fetch hundreds of keys in parallel, making this a real risk: all the cache servers reply together to one web server. Meta's clients use flow control, a sliding window that limits the number of outstanding requests, so responses arrive in manageable waves instead of one burst that the switch cannot buffer.
deeper:
Incast is a consequence of fan-out. When one web server requests hundreds of keys spread across many cache servers, those servers are each fast and each reply immediately, so their responses converge on the same switch port at nearly the same instant. Switch buffers are finite; once full, packets are dropped. Dropped packets mean retransmissions or, for UDP gets, false misses, both of which hurt latency.

A sliding window caps how many requests are outstanding at any moment. Too small a window and the client serializes requests, adding latency; too large and incast returns. The window lets the client keep the network busy without overwhelming it.

The chapter's failure-mode list generalizes the point: a page that fetches 500 keys waits for the slowest, so batch requests, cap fan-out, and watch incast. Large values make it worse because each response carries more bytes into the same buffers. Fan-out is thus both a latency problem and a network capacity problem.

quiz.q: What is incast congestion and how did Meta's clients avoid it?
quiz.a: Many simultaneous responses to one client overflow switch buffers. Clients use a sliding window limiting outstanding requests so replies arrive in manageable waves.

title: Pools: stop churny keys from evicting valuable ones
body: Meta splits its memcached servers into pools: separate groups of servers for workloads with different access patterns. The goal is isolation. A low-value, high-churn key set, one that is written often and rarely re-read, would otherwise push valuable, frequently read keys out of memory in a shared cache. By giving each workload its own pool, eviction pressure from one workload cannot destroy another workload's hit ratio. mcrouter routes each key to the right pool by key prefix.
deeper:
Caches evict when memory fills. In a shared cache, the keys that survive are whatever the eviction policy favors, and a workload that writes lots of keys can dominate memory even if nobody reads them twice. The keys it pushes out may be exactly the ones that were saving the database the most load.

Pools also let each workload get the right treatment. Keys with very high read rates can go into a replicated pool, where each key has copies on several servers, which is how Meta spreads hot keys. Large, less popular items go into a shared regional pool rather than being duplicated in every frontend cluster.

The failure-mode section names the problem 'eviction surprises': a new feature writes many low-value keys and evicts valuable ones. The fix it recommends is separate pools, as at Meta, or separate clusters per workload. It is an operational lesson too: launching a new caching workload into a shared cache can silently raise database load for an unrelated service.

quiz.q: Why does Meta use separate pools for different workloads?
quiz.a: So a low-value, high-churn workload cannot evict another workload's valuable keys, protecting each workload's hit ratio.

title: The Gutter pool: 1% idle servers cut failures by 99%
body: Meta keeps about 1 percent of memcached servers idle as a Gutter pool. When a cache server fails, clients send its traffic to Gutter instead of rehashing its keys onto other servers in the cluster. Rehashing could push a hot key onto a healthy server and overload it, causing a cascade. Gutter entries expire quickly, limiting staleness since Gutter gets no normal invalidations. This small reserve cut client-visible failures by 99 percent.
deeper:
The naive failure response in a consistent-hashing cluster is to remap the dead server's keys to its neighbors. The problem is uneven load: if the dead server held a hot key, a neighbor suddenly receives that key's traffic on top of its own, may fail, and push the load onward. The failure-mode section calls this failure rehashing: a hot key can overload the next node, which dies, and so on.

Gutter breaks the chain. The failed server's traffic goes to dedicated idle servers that have spare capacity by design, so no healthy server's load changes. Misses to Gutter are filled from the database, and the short expiry keeps any stale data short-lived.

The cost is holding roughly 1 in 100 servers mostly idle, a small price for a 99 percent reduction in client-visible failures. The chapter's failure cascade diagram lists the Gutter pool alongside warm restart and cold cluster warmup as the mitigations for the first stage: cache nodes restarting or failing and the hit ratio dropping.

quiz.q: Why is rehashing a failed cache node's keys onto other nodes risky, and what did Meta do instead?
quiz.a: Load per key is uneven, so a moved hot key can overload a healthy node and cascade. Meta sends failed nodes' traffic to a small idle Gutter pool with short TTLs.

title: Across clusters and regions: duplication, sharing, markers
body: Within a Meta region, several frontend clusters share one storage cluster. Each frontend cluster has its own full cache, so popular data is duplicated across clusters. Less popular, large items go into a shared regional pool to save memory. Across regions, one region holds the primary databases and others hold replicas. McSqueal invalidations flow along with MySQL replication, and remote markers protect read-after-write for users in non-primary regions by sending their reads to the primary region.
deeper:
The per-cluster full cache is a deliberate trade. Duplicating popular data costs memory, but it keeps each frontend cluster self-contained: web servers read from nearby cache servers and a failure in one cluster does not affect others. For popular keys, the extra copies also spread load.

For large, rarely read items the trade flips. Duplicating them in every cluster wastes a lot of memory for little hit-ratio benefit, so they go into one shared regional pool, used by all frontend clusters in the region.

Invalidation must reach every copy. McSqueal on each database extracts keys from committed SQL and broadcasts deletes to all frontend clusters in the region, batched through mcrouter. Across regions, those invalidations travel with MySQL replication, so a replica region's caches are cleaned in step with its data.

The cross-region read-after-write gap is covered by remote markers: a writer in a non-primary region sets a marker in the regional cache, writes to the primary database, and deletes the local key; readers seeing the marker go to the primary region.

quiz.q: Why does Meta put large, less popular items in a shared regional pool rather than in each frontend cluster's cache?
quiz.a: Duplicating them in every cluster wastes memory for little hit-ratio gain; one shared pool per region saves memory, while popular data stays duplicated per cluster.

title: Cold Cluster Warmup: hours instead of days
body: When a new Meta frontend cluster comes online, its cache is empty, and sending all its misses to the database would be dangerous. Cold Cluster Warmup lets the cold cluster read its misses from a warm cluster's cache instead of the database. This brings the new cluster to full capacity in a few hours instead of a few days. To avoid races during warmup, deletes to the cold cluster carry a two-second hold-off, preventing stale data from being refilled.
deeper:
Why is a cold cluster dangerous? A cache at 99 percent hit ratio sends 1 percent of reads to the database; an empty cache sends 100 percent. A new cluster serving real traffic with an empty cache would multiply database load until it filled, and filling from the database alone takes days for the long tail of keys.

Warmup redirects those misses to a peer cluster that already holds the data, since each frontend cluster has its own full cache of similar content. The database is spared, and the cold cluster fills far faster.

The race: the cold cluster fetches a value from the warm cluster, while a write deletes that key in both. If the warm cluster's copy was fetched just before its delete, the cold cluster could set stale data just after its own delete. The two-second hold-off rejects sets for a key for a short time after it is deleted in the cold cluster, closing that window.

The failure-mode section lists cold cluster warmup from a warm peer among the mitigations for cold caches after restarts or deploys.

quiz.q: How does Meta's Cold Cluster Warmup protect the database, and why the two-second hold-off?
quiz.a: The cold cluster reads misses from a warm cluster instead of the database. The hold-off on deletes prevents a warm-cluster fetch from refilling a just-deleted key with stale data.

title: TAO: a cache that understands the social graph
body: TAO later took over many social-graph reads from Meta's memcache layer. Unlike memcached, TAO is a cache that understands the graph model of nodes and edges. Follower tiers serve client requests. Leader tiers, one per shard, read and write MySQL and send invalidations to the followers. Because all writes to a shard go through one leader, TAO avoids many look-aside races by design. It handled a billion reads per second in 2013.
deeper:
TAO shows an alternative to patching look-aside races one by one. In the memcache design, many independent web servers read the database, fill the cache and send deletes, and races arise from their uncoordinated interleaving: stale sets, lost invalidations, and ordering problems. Leases, McSqueal and remote markers were added to manage them.

In TAO, the leader for a shard is the single path for writes to that shard's data. It writes MySQL and then invalidates the follower tiers, so there is one ordered stream of changes per shard rather than many competing clients. Followers serve reads and ask the leader on misses. Serializing writes through a leader removes much of the ambiguity about which update came last.

Understanding the data model also helps: the cache knows about graph objects and associations rather than opaque keys, fitting Meta's graph-heavy workload. It is a precursor to the integrated-cache trend the chapter highlights with Uber's CacheFront: when the data platform owns the cache, application code cannot forget to invalidate.

quiz.q: Why does TAO avoid many look-aside races by design?
quiz.a: All writes to a shard go through one leader tier that writes MySQL and invalidates followers, giving a single ordered write path instead of many uncoordinated clients.

title: CacheLib: one caching engine instead of many rebuilt ones
body: By 2017 Meta had many separate caching systems, for the CDN, the social graph, storage and application caches, each with its own team rebuilding the same features. CacheLib is a C++ caching library that extracts the common core so every system can share it. First deployed in 2017, it powered over 70 services by 2020, as described in its OSDI 2020 paper. Its standout ideas are hybrid DRAM plus flash caching, flash-friendly storage engines, admission policies and warm restarts.
deeper:
The motivation is engineering economics. Each caching team was independently implementing eviction, memory management, concurrency, persistence across restarts and flash support. Features built by one team did not help another, and bugs were fixed many times over. A shared library turns those into common investments: an improvement in CacheLib benefits every service that links it.

CacheLib is a library, not a server, which is why it could slot into so many different systems, from CDN edge caches to social-graph caches to storage caches. Each service keeps its own protocol and deployment while sharing the caching engine.

The paper also made two contributions beyond the code. It quantified cache benefits, noting that a single caching server can replace tens of backend database servers thanks to about 20 times higher throughput and hit ratios above 80 percent. And it measured real production workloads, finding popularity less skewed and more volatile than textbook models, which strengthens the case for larger caches and therefore for flash. Meta's CDN edge caches, which serve 70 percent of web requests, are among its users.

quiz.q: Why did Meta build CacheLib as a shared library?
quiz.a: Many separate caching systems were each rebuilding the same features; a common C++ core let over 70 services share one engine and its improvements.

title: Hybrid DRAM plus flash: more cache per dollar
body: CacheLib caches in two tiers: DRAM first, then flash. DRAM is fast but expensive and limited in size. Flash (SSD) gives many times more capacity per dollar and still offers sub-millisecond reads. On a lookup, CacheLib checks DRAM first; on a DRAM miss it checks flash before falling back to the backend. The result is a much bigger cache for the same budget, able to hold far more of the long tail of less popular items.
deeper:
The economics come from the long tail. Hot items fit in DRAM, but many workloads have a large set of items that are each read occasionally. Keeping them in DRAM is too expensive; letting them miss sends a steady stream of reads to the backend. Flash sits in between: slower than DRAM but much faster than a database read that touches disk and replicas.

Flash brings two engineering problems that shape CacheLib's design. Endurance: flash wears out with writes, and cache contents churn fast, so writing every evicted item would burn through devices. Admission policies control this. Indexing: keeping a DRAM index entry for every item on a large flash device can cost too much DRAM, especially for small items. The Small Object Cache avoids a per-item index.

The chapter's senior staff lens frames the payoff: when the working set is 10 times bigger than affordable DRAM, a DRAM-only cache has a poor hit ratio and the backend pays, while DRAM plus flash can hold the long tail.

quiz.q: What does adding a flash tier behind DRAM buy a cache?
quiz.a: Many times more capacity per dollar with sub-millisecond reads, so the long tail of less popular items can be served from cache instead of the backend.

title: LOC and SOC: two flash engines for big and tiny items
body: CacheLib uses two flash engines. The Large Object Cache (LOC) stores items of 2 KB and larger, aligned to 4 KB flash pages, and keeps a compact index in DRAM to find them. The Small Object Cache (SOC) stores items under 2 KB by hashing them into 4 KB buckets on flash, so it needs almost no DRAM index. Small objects, like social-graph edges and nodes, are very common, so avoiding a per-item DRAM index matters enormously.
deeper:
Why two engines? The cost of indexing grows with the number of items, not their size. For large items, an index entry per item is a tiny overhead relative to the data, so LOC can afford a DRAM index and place each item directly on page-aligned flash.

For small items, a per-item index would be ruinous. A flash device holds a huge number of sub-2 KB objects, and a DRAM entry for each could approach the size of the objects themselves, defeating the point of using flash to save DRAM. SOC sidesteps this: an item's key hashes to one 4 KB bucket on flash, so the location is computed rather than looked up. Reading an item means reading its bucket and searching within it.

The layouts also matter for flash wear. The chapter's quiz answer lists flash layouts designed to limit application-level write amplification as one of two ways CacheLib reduces wear, alongside admission policies. Aligning writes to 4 KB flash pages and buckets fits how the device works.

quiz.q: Why does CacheLib's Small Object Cache hash items into 4 KB flash buckets instead of indexing each item in DRAM?
quiz.a: Small items are extremely numerous, so a per-item DRAM index would cost too much; hashing to a bucket computes the location and needs almost no DRAM.

title: Flash admission: don't write every evicted item
body: Flash wears out with writes, and cache contents churn quickly. If every item evicted from DRAM were written to flash, the devices would wear out fast. CacheLib therefore uses admission policies: it does not write every evicted item to flash. The default policy admits items with a fixed probability, for example writing only some fraction of candidates. That gives operators direct control over the flash write rate, and therefore over device lifetime, at the cost of not caching some items on flash.
deeper:
Admission is the core trade-off of flash caching. Admit everything and you maximize the chance of a flash hit but burn flash endurance; admit too little and flash sits underused while the backend pays for misses. A probabilistic policy is simple and predictable: the write rate scales directly with the admission probability, so you can set it to match the device's endurance budget.

The chapter's quiz asks for two ways CacheLib reduces flash wear: probabilistic (or other) admission policies that write only some evicted items to flash, and flash layouts, LOC and SOC, designed to limit application-level write amplification.

The senior staff lens on flash caches names the cost directly: flash endurance must be managed by controlling the write rate with admission policies, and flash hits carry slightly higher latency than DRAM hits. The key takeaways repeat the point: flash caching extends cache capacity cheaply, but control flash writes with admission policies. Aerospike's hybrid layout faces a related trade-off as a database rather than a cache.

quiz.q: Name two ways CacheLib reduces flash wear.
quiz.a: Admission policies that write only some evicted items to flash (default: fixed probability), and flash layouts (LOC and SOC) that limit write amplification.

title: Warm restarts: deploys shouldn't empty the cache
body: Production caches restart often, mainly for code deploys; many of Meta's run less than 7 days between restarts. A normal restart leaves the cache empty, forcing it to refill from the backend and hitting the database hard. CacheLib supports warm restarts: it can save its state before shutting down and reattach to it after the restart, so the cache comes back full instead of empty. Frequent deploys then no longer mean frequent cold caches and database load spikes.
deeper:
