The problem compounds with scale. If each cache server restarts every few days, then at any time some fraction of the fleet is cold and refilling. Restart many at once, as in a fleet-wide deploy, and the database sees a surge. The failure-mode section lists cold cache after restart or deploy as the first failure mode, with mitigations: roll restarts slowly, warm restarts (CacheLib), cold cluster warmup from a warm peer (Meta), and cross-region replication (EVCache, CacheFront).

Warm restarts are the cheapest of these because the data never leaves the machine. Rather than rebuilding from the database or copying from another cluster, the process hands off its saved state to the new version.

This matters more for large caches. A DRAM plus flash cache holding the long tail takes a long time to fill organically because long-tail items are, by definition, rarely requested. Losing that on every deploy would erase much of the benefit of having a big cache in the first place.

quiz.q: Why are warm restarts especially valuable for caches that are deployed frequently?
quiz.a: Each normal restart empties the cache and spikes database load while refilling; saving and reattaching state lets frequent deploys keep caches full.

title: Real workloads aren't very Zipf: the case for big caches
body: The CacheLib paper measured real production workloads and found that popularity is often less skewed than the textbook Zipf assumption. The social-graph and CDN workloads had a Zipf alpha around 0.55, meaning traffic is spread across more items instead of concentrating on a few. Popularity also changes quickly, over hours. Both findings make caching harder and larger caches more valuable, because a small cache of the top items misses a lot. That is the case for flash.
deeper:
Zipf distributions model popularity where a few items get most of the traffic. The steeper the skew, the more a small cache of the most popular items can capture. With a flatter distribution like alpha around 0.55, the hit ratio grows more slowly with cache size: to catch most requests you need to hold a much larger share of the items.

Fast-changing popularity adds churn: yesterday's hot items cool off and new ones appear within hours, so the cache is constantly replacing contents, which also increases write pressure on flash.

Together these push toward bigger caches, and bigger caches are affordable only with cheaper media. That is why the paper connects its measurements to flash: DRAM plus flash can hold the long tail that a DRAM-only cache cannot afford. The sizing section shows why each point of hit ratio matters so much: in the running example, every 1 percent of hit ratio gained removes 20,000 database reads per second at peak.

quiz.q: Why does a less skewed popularity distribution make larger (flash) caches more valuable?
quiz.a: Traffic spreads over more items, so a small cache of top items catches less; holding more of the long tail is needed for a good hit ratio, which flash makes affordable.

title: Aerospike: index in DRAM, records on SSD, one flash read
body: Aerospike applies a related idea to a database rather than a cache. Its Hybrid Memory Architecture keeps the primary index in DRAM and the records themselves on SSD. Because the index is always in memory, finding a record never needs a flash read, and fetching it needs exactly one. So every lookup costs at most one flash read. It gets much of the speed of an in-memory store at the capacity and cost of flash, while still being a durable store.
deeper:
The comparison with CacheLib's Large Object Cache is instructive: both keep a compact index in DRAM and the bulk of the data on flash, so a lookup goes straight to the right flash location. The difference is role. CacheLib is a cache that can lose data and refill from a backend; Aerospike is a database, so the records on SSD are the real data.

The design gives predictable latency, since the worst case is a single flash read, not a chain of index page reads from disk as a B-tree on SSD might require. The trade-off is DRAM cost for the index: it scales with the number of records, which is exactly the problem CacheLib's Small Object Cache avoids for tiny items by hashing into buckets instead.

The key takeaways group it with CacheLib: flash caching and Aerospike-style layouts extend capacity cheaply, provided you control flash writes. It shows the same hardware economics shaping both caches and primary stores.

quiz.q: How does Aerospike's Hybrid Memory Architecture guarantee at most one flash read per lookup?
quiz.a: The primary index lives entirely in DRAM, so locating a record needs no flash access; only reading the record itself touches the SSD.

title: Senior lens: flash caches change the cost curve
body: Flash caches change the cost curve of caching. When the working set is 10 times bigger than affordable DRAM, a DRAM-only cache has a poor hit ratio, and the backend database pays for all those misses. A DRAM plus flash cache can hold the long tail instead. The costs are flash endurance, which must be controlled through admission policies that limit write rate, and slightly higher latency for hits served from flash rather than DRAM.
deeper:
The key question a senior reviewer asks is: how big is the working set relative to what DRAM we can afford? If the hot set fits comfortably in DRAM, flash adds complexity for little gain. If the working set is much larger, which the CacheLib measurements suggest is common because real popularity is less skewed and changes quickly, then DRAM-only caching leaves a big hit-ratio gap that shows up as database load.

The sizing math makes this concrete. Database load equals read rate times one minus hit ratio, so small gains in hit ratio remove large amounts of database work. In the chapter's example, every 1 percent of hit ratio gained removes 20,000 database reads per second at peak, and the full 1 billion profile set of about 1.1 TB could fit in a few flash-backed servers.

The costs are manageable when designed for: pick an admission probability matching device endurance, and accept that a flash hit is slower than DRAM but still far faster than a database read.

quiz.q: When does a DRAM plus flash cache beat a DRAM-only cache, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: When the working set far exceeds affordable DRAM, flash holds the long tail and raises hit ratio. Costs: flash endurance (limit writes via admission) and slightly slower flash hits.

title: EVCache: memcached for AWS, a full copy per zone
body: EVCache, short for Ephemeral Volatile Cache, is Netflix's distributed cache built on memcached and designed for AWS. Clients use consistent hashing (the Ketama algorithm) to spread keys across servers. A typical setup keeps a full copy of the data in each availability zone. Reads go to the local zone, which keeps latency low. Writes go to all zones. If an item is missing locally, because of an instance failure or eviction, the client can read it from another zone.
deeper:
The per-zone copy design addresses several of the chapter's problems at once. Latency: reads stay inside the zone, avoiding cross-zone network hops. Availability: losing a cache instance or even a whole zone does not mean a cold cache, since other zones still hold the data and the client can fall back to them. Hot keys: because every zone has a copy, reads for a popular key are naturally spread across zones.

The cost is memory and write fan-out. Every item is stored once per zone, and every write or delete must reach every zone. The sizing section's example uses the same shape: one copy per zone in three zones triples the memory needed, from about 220 GB to about 660 GB.

Putting the replication logic in the client keeps the servers as plain memcached. The client handles hashing, zone selection, writing to all zones, and fallback reads. That same client is also where Netflix hooks in cross-region replication, publishing metadata events so other regions' caches stay warm.

quiz.q: Why does EVCache keep a full copy of the data in each availability zone?
quiz.a: So reads stay local and fast, a missing item can be read from another zone after failure or eviction, and zone loss doesn't leave a cold cache.

title: EVCache's cross-region pipeline: ship keys, not values
body: Netflix runs active in several AWS regions and can move all traffic out of a failing region. If the target region's caches were cold, the sudden traffic would crush its databases, so EVCache replicates across regions. The app writes to its local EVCache. The client publishes a small metadata event, the key but not the value, to Kafka. A replication reader consumes it, reads the latest value from local EVCache, and sends it to a replication writer in the other region, which writes it there.
deeper:
Sending only metadata through Kafka keeps the pipeline small: keys are tiny compared to values, so Kafka carries far less data. There is also a correctness benefit. Because the reader fetches the value from local EVCache when it processes the event, it always replicates the newest value, not whatever was current when the event was published. If a key is written several times quickly, each event results in shipping the latest state.

The scale reported in 2024 shows why efficiency matters: about 200 memcached clusters, 22,000 server instances, 400 million operations per second, 30 million replication events globally, and about 2 trillion items totaling 14.3 PB.

The pipeline covers both sets and deletes, so the remote region's cache tracks the local one. Uber's CacheFront takes a similar approach for failover, replicating Redis writes so the remote region has a warm cache. The chapter's quiz asks exactly this: EVCache sends only metadata (the key and operation) because it keeps messages small and always replicates the newest value.

quiz.q: What does EVCache send through Kafka for cross-region replication, and why not the value itself?
quiz.a: Only metadata (key and operation). The reader fetches the latest value from local EVCache, keeping Kafka messages small and always replicating the newest value.

title: Netflix: the warm cache is part of disaster recovery
body: Netflix's approach treats the cache as part of its disaster-recovery plan. When a region fails, Netflix moves all its traffic to other regions. The caches in the failover region are kept warm on purpose through cross-region replication, because a cold cache during failover would turn a regional outage into a global database overload. The failover region must absorb extra traffic, and a warm cache ensures that extra traffic mostly hits memory instead of landing on the databases.
deeper:
This is the load-bearing cache idea taken to its logical end. A region's databases are sized for that region's normal miss traffic. During failover, the surviving region suddenly serves users from the failed region too. If those users' data is not in the local cache, every one of their reads misses, and the combined miss rate can far exceed what the databases can take. The outage would spread from one region to all of them.

Keeping caches warm across regions costs continuous replication traffic and memory in every region, whether or not a failover ever happens. Netflix pays that cost because failover must actually work when it is needed.

The key takeaways generalize the lesson: warm caches are part of disaster recovery, and both Netflix EVCache and Uber CacheFront replicate caches across regions for failover. The failure-mode section lists cross-region replication among the mitigations for cold caches, alongside slow rolling restarts, CacheLib warm restarts and Meta's cold cluster warmup.

quiz.q: Why would a cold cache in the failover region risk turning a regional outage into a global one?
quiz.a: Redirected traffic would all miss and hit the surviving region's databases, overloading them and spreading the failure beyond the original region.

title: Twemcache: Twitter's operational fork of memcached
body: Twitter ran large memcached fleets and forked memcached 1.4.4 into Twemcache. The changes were mainly operational. It added pluggable eviction strategies: item LRU, random eviction, and slab-level eviction to handle slab calcification, where memory stays stuck in size classes that no longer match the workload. It also added lock-free stats and a lockless command logger for debugging. Twemcache was retired in 2021 in favor of Pelikan, Twitter's newer cache framework.
deeper:
Slab calcification needs a little background. Memcached allocates memory in slabs divided into fixed size classes, and items go into the class that fits them. If the workload's item sizes shift over time, memory already assigned to old size classes can remain there even though new items need a different class. The cache is effectively smaller than its memory, and hit ratio suffers. Slab-level eviction frees whole slabs so memory can move to the size classes that need it now.

The other changes target running caches at scale. Lock-free statistics let operators observe the cache without adding contention on hot paths. A lockless command logger allows capturing what commands a server is receiving to debug problems in production without slowing it down.

The theme is consistent with the chapter's senior lens on Twitter: at scale, a cache's memory efficiency and operational behavior matter as much as raw speed. Pelikan and its Segcache engine continued that line of work.

quiz.q: What is slab calcification, and how did Twemcache handle it?
quiz.a: Memory stays stuck in slab size classes that no longer match the workload's item sizes. Twemcache added slab-level eviction to free and reuse that memory.

title: Pelikan and Segcache: expire by the segment, not the item
body: Pelikan is Twitter's framework for building cache servers from shared, reusable parts, now written in Rust. It separates control plane and data plane at runtime and uses lockless data structures so worker threads never block. Its Segcache storage engine (NSDI 2021) groups objects with similar expiry times into segments, so expired data is removed in bulk. Segcache used 22 to 60 percent less memory than state-of-the-art designs on tested workloads and scaled to close to 8 times memcached's throughput at 24 threads.
deeper:
Why does grouping by expiry help? In a typical cache, items with different TTLs are mixed together, so expired items linger in memory until something happens to look at them, and removing them one by one is costly. Segcache places objects with similar expiry times into the same segment. When a segment's time comes, the whole segment is dropped at once, reclaiming memory promptly and cheaply.

The memory savings, 22 to 60 percent less than state-of-the-art designs on the tested workloads, come partly from this prompt expiration and from reducing per-object overhead for small objects, the engine's focus.

The throughput result, close to 8 times memcached at 24 threads, reflects Pelikan's design goal that worker threads never block, using lockless data structures and keeping control-plane work off the data path.

The framework approach echoes CacheLib's motivation at Meta: build cache servers from shared, reusable parts instead of every team starting from scratch. Pelikan replaced Twemcache at Twitter in 2021.

quiz.q: How does Segcache reclaim expired data more efficiently than per-item expiry?
quiz.a: It groups objects with similar expiry times into segments and removes whole segments at once when they expire, instead of finding and deleting items individually.

title: Senior lens: 50 bytes per item is terabytes at trillions
body: Twitter's lesson is that at scale, a cache's memory efficiency and TTL handling matter as much as raw speed. Per-object metadata overhead of 50 bytes is nothing for one item, but across trillions of items it becomes many terabytes of RAM. That is memory you pay for without caching any data. Designs that shave metadata per item, and that reclaim expired items promptly, can let the same hardware hold far more of the working set.
deeper:
Run the numbers in the spirit of the chapter: one trillion items times 50 bytes of metadata each is 50 TB of RAM spent purely on bookkeeping. Netflix's EVCache alone held about 2 trillion items in 2024, so the scale is real.

Memory efficiency converts directly into hit ratio. With the same DRAM, a leaner engine holds more items, which raises the hit ratio, which lowers database load. And the sizing section shows how leveraged that is: in the running example each 1 percent of hit ratio is 20,000 database reads per second at peak.

TTL handling matters for the same reason. Expired items that sit in memory until evicted are dead weight; an engine like Segcache that removes them in bulk frees memory for live data. Small objects make overhead proportionally worse, which is why both Segcache and CacheLib's Small Object Cache focus on them. The sizing example itself assumes about 100 bytes of cache overhead on each 1 KB profile, roughly 10 percent.

quiz.q: Why does per-object metadata overhead matter so much in very large caches?
quiz.a: Small overhead multiplied by trillions of items consumes terabytes of RAM that could hold data, lowering hit ratio and raising backend load.

section: 6.10 Uber CacheFront: a cache inside the database
title: Uber CacheFront: the database query engine owns the cache
body: Instead of every team building its own look-aside logic, Uber put the cache inside Docstore's query engine. This is CacheFront (2024). On reads, the query engine checks Redis first, returns cached rows, fetches the rest from the storage engine, and fills Redis asynchronously. For invalidation, Flux tails the MySQL binlog and invalidates or updates Redis within seconds, and the write path also invalidates directly so reads are fresh sooner. Applications just query Docstore and get caching automatically.
deeper:
CacheFront is a read-through cache in the chapter's pattern table: the cache layer, not the application, fills on a miss. Placing it in the query engine means every Docstore user gets the same well-tested behavior.

The read path handles partial hits naturally. A query for several rows returns the cached ones from Redis and fetches only the missing rows from storage. Filling Redis asynchronously keeps the fill off the request's critical path.

Invalidation uses two channels. The direct invalidation from the write path gives fast freshness in the normal case. Flux, tailing the binlog, is the reliable backstop: because the binlog is durable and ordered, a crashed write path cannot cause a lost invalidation. This mirrors Meta's McSqueal, which also invalidates from the commit log.

On top of that, CacheFront guards against stale fills with timestamp checks, caches missing rows, shards Redis independently of the database, and replicates to other regions, each covered on the following cards.

quiz.q: Why does CacheFront invalidate both from the write path and from Flux tailing the binlog?
quiz.a: Direct invalidation gives fresh reads quickly; the binlog-driven Flux is durable and ordered, so invalidations are never lost if the write path fails.

section: 6.10 Uber CacheFront: a cache inside the database
title: Timestamp guards and negative caching in CacheFront
body: CacheFront adds two protections on top of basic caching. Stale-fill protection: Lua scripts in Redis compare row timestamps so older data can never overwrite newer data, closing the late-fill race where a slow reader writes old values after a fresher update. Negative caching: rows that do not exist are cached with a flag marking them as missing, so repeated lookups for keys that are absent do not each hit MySQL. Both reduce database load and stale reads without any application code.
deeper:
The timestamp check is Uber's answer to the stale-set race that Meta solved with leases. Instead of tokens, each cached row carries its timestamp, and a Lua script, which runs atomically inside Redis, only writes the incoming row if it is newer than what is already there. A delayed asynchronous fill or a lagging source cannot resurrect old data.

Negative caching targets a subtle load source. Without it, a lookup for a row that does not exist always misses, because there is nothing to cache, and always goes to the database. If many requests look up missing rows repeatedly, perhaps due to a client bug or a common probe pattern, the database takes that load in full no matter how high the hit ratio is for existing rows. Caching the absence with a flag turns those into cache hits.

Negative entries must also be invalidated when the row is later created, which the binlog-driven Flux path covers, since row creation is a committed write.

quiz.q: What problem does negative caching solve in CacheFront?
quiz.a: Lookups for rows that don't exist would always miss and hit MySQL; caching a 'missing' flag lets repeated lookups for absent keys be served from Redis.

section: 6.10 Uber CacheFront: a cache inside the database
title: Shard the cache apart from the database, warm it across regions
body: CacheFront shards Redis by partition key, independently of how the database is sharded. If one Redis cluster fails, its misses spread across all database shards instead of hammering one. CacheFront also replicates Redis writes to a remote region, so that region has a warm cache ready for failover, the same idea as Netflix EVCache. Both choices are about making cache failures survivable: a single cache failure should not overload one database shard, and a region failover should not start cold.
deeper:
The sharding choice is subtle. If Redis clusters mapped one-to-one onto database shards, a Redis cluster failure would send its entire miss load to exactly one database shard, which is sized for only its normal miss traffic. By sharding independently, each Redis cluster holds keys from many database shards, so its failure spreads a modest increase across all of them. The blast radius per database shard stays small.

This is a concrete answer to the senior staff question from the start of the chapter: if this cache were empty, could the database survive? For a single cluster failure, spreading misses makes the answer yes more often.

Cross-region warming handles the larger failure: losing a region. Like EVCache, replicating cache writes means the failover region's Redis already holds the data users from the failed region will request. The key takeaways put Netflix and Uber together on this point: warm caches are part of disaster recovery.

quiz.q: Why does CacheFront shard Redis independently of database sharding?
quiz.a: So a failed Redis cluster's misses spread across all database shards rather than overloading the one shard it would otherwise mirror.

section: 6.10 Uber CacheFront: a cache inside the database
title: CacheFront results: 40M reads/sec, 99.99% consistency
body: Uber reported CacheFront's results in 2024: over 40 million reads per second across instances, cache hit rates up to 99 percent in production cases, p75 latency down 75 percent, p99.9 latency down more than 67 percent, and consistency measured at 99.99 percent. CacheFront illustrates the integrated-cache trend: when the database platform owns the cache, invalidation comes from the commit log, every team gets caching for free, and application code cannot forget to delete a key.
deeper:
Each number maps to a design choice. The hit rate up to 99 percent reflects caching done centrally with negative caching, so even missing rows hit. The latency drops, 75 percent at p75 and more than 67 percent at p99.9, show the tail improving along with the median, as expected when most reads move from storage to memory. The 99.99 percent consistency figure reflects the layered defenses: direct invalidation, binlog-driven Flux, and Lua timestamp checks against stale fills.

One CacheFront use case also produced the chapter's cost example: 6 million reads per second on about 3,000 Redis cores versus an estimated 60,000 database cores.

The integrated-cache trend addresses the organizational weakness of look-aside caching. When every team implements its own cache logic, some team will eventually forget a delete, skip the TTL or mishandle a race. Meta's TAO took a similar route for the social graph. Moving the cache into the data platform turns correctness into a platform property instead of a per-team discipline.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of an integrated cache like CacheFront over per-team look-aside caches?
quiz.a: The platform owns invalidation from the commit log and all protections, so every team gets correct caching for free and no application can forget to delete a key.

title: Redis and Valkey: data structures in memory
body: Redis is an in-memory data-structure server. Beyond plain strings it supports hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and streams. That makes it popular both as a cache and as a small primary store, for things like leaderboards, rate limiters and sessions. In 2024 the Linux Foundation community forked Redis as Valkey, which keeps compatibility with the Redis protocol and cluster design. Everything about clustering and persistence in this section applies to both.
deeper:
The data-structure model is what separates Redis from memcached's plain get, set and delete. A sorted set can keep a leaderboard ordered by score, a counter can be incremented atomically for rate limiting, and a hash can store a session's fields. Server-side scripts in Lua can run atomically, which is how Uber's CacheFront implements its timestamp comparisons to block stale fills.

Using Redis as a primary store is where care is needed. Its replication is asynchronous and its persistence modes can lose recent writes, so the chapter's common mistake box warns against treating it as a durable database just because persistence is on. The safe uses are data you can lose or rebuild.

Valkey's compatibility means existing clients and cluster setups keep working. At large scale, Redis-style caches are proven: Uber's CacheFront serves over 40 million reads per second backed by Redis. The next cards cover cluster mode (hash slots, redirection, replicas) and the persistence options.

quiz.q: What makes Redis more than a plain key-value cache, and what are common non-cache uses?
quiz.a: It stores data structures like hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and streams, so it is used as a small primary store for leaderboards, rate limiters and sessions.

title: 16,384 hash slots and the {hash tag} trick
body: Redis and Valkey cluster mode split the key space into 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each primary node owns some slots. Moving data between nodes means moving slots. Hash tags control placement: if a key contains braces, only the part inside the braces is hashed. So {user1000}.followers and {user1000}.following land in the same slot, on the same node, and can be used together in one multi-key operation.
deeper:
Why slots instead of hashing keys directly to nodes? Slots add a fixed layer of indirection. The key-to-slot mapping never changes, since it is just CRC16 mod 16384. Only the slot-to-node mapping changes when nodes are added or removed, so rebalancing moves whole slots rather than recomputing every key's home.

Multi-key operations need all keys on the same node, because a single node executes the command. Without hash tags, related keys would scatter across the cluster by their full names and could not be used in one operation. Hash tags let the application group related keys deliberately: everything about user1000 shares a slot.

The flip side is that hash tags can create hotspots. Everything with the same tag lives in one slot on one node, so grouping too much under one tag, or tagging a very popular entity, recreates the hot-key problem from earlier in the chapter, which sharding cannot fix. Use tags for keys that genuinely need to be operated on together.

quiz.q: Why would you put {user1000} in braces in Redis Cluster keys?
quiz.a: Only the braced part is hashed, so all keys with that tag land in the same slot and node, enabling multi-key operations on them.

title: MOVED vs ASK: how Redis clients follow slots around
body: Redis Cluster clients cache the slot map, knowing which node owns each slot, so they can send requests directly to the right node. When the map is out of date, the node replies with a redirect. A MOVED reply means the slot has moved permanently to another node: the client should update its cached map. An ASK reply means the slot is currently migrating: the client should try the other node for just this request, without updating its map.
deeper:
The distinction exists because slot migration is gradual. While a slot moves from node A to node B, some of its keys are already on B and some are still on A. A request for a key that has already moved gets ASK: go to B for this one. The client should not rewrite its map yet, because other keys of that slot may still be on A. Once migration finishes, the cluster reassigns the slot, and requests to A get MOVED, telling the client to update its map permanently.

Client-side slot maps avoid a proxy hop on every request, similar to how Meta's clients hash keys to servers and EVCache clients use Ketama consistent hashing. The cost is that clients must handle redirects correctly. A client that treated ASK like MOVED would redirect all of a slot's keys to B too early, and one that ignored MOVED would keep paying an extra hop on every request.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a MOVED and an ASK reply in Redis Cluster?
quiz.a: MOVED: the slot moved permanently, so update the cached slot map. ASK: the slot is migrating, so try the other node for this request only, without updating the map.

title: Async replication: Redis can lose acknowledged writes
body: Each Redis Cluster primary has replicas, but replication is asynchronous. The primary acknowledges a write to the client before replicas have received it. If the primary then fails and a replica is promoted, that write may never have reached the replica, so it is gone even though the client was told it succeeded. The cluster can also lose acknowledged writes on the minority side of a network partition. Redis Cluster does not guarantee acknowledged writes survive failover.
deeper:
Asynchronous replication is a latency choice. Waiting for replicas before acknowledging would add a network round trip to every write, and Redis is built for speed. For a pure cache, losing a few recent writes during failover is harmless: the data can be read again from the source of truth.

The partition case is less obvious. If a network split leaves a primary on the minority side, clients connected to it may keep writing for a while. When the majority promotes a replica on its side, the minority primary's writes during the split are discarded.

The chapter's quiz frames it directly: a primary acknowledges a write and fails before replicating it. The write can be lost, because replication is asynchronous, the promoted replica may not have it, and the cluster does not guarantee survival of acknowledged writes. Combined with persistence settings like fsync every second, this is why the chapter warns against treating Redis as a strongly durable database.

quiz.q: A Redis Cluster primary acknowledges a write, then fails before replicating it. What happens to the write, and why?
quiz.a: It can be lost. Replication is asynchronous, so the promoted replica may never have received it; the cluster doesn't guarantee acknowledged writes survive failover.

title: RDB vs AOF: how much can Redis forget on restart?
body: Redis offers several persistence modes. RDB snapshots are periodic point-in-time dumps made using fork(): compact and fast to restart from, but you can lose minutes of writes, and fork() on a big dataset can pause the server briefly. AOF, the append-only file, logs every write: with the default fsync every second, you can lose about one second of writes, while fsync always is very safe and very slow. You can combine RDB plus AOF, or use no persistence, common for pure caches.
deeper:
The modes trade restart speed, write overhead and data loss. RDB writes a full snapshot occasionally, so it is cheap during normal operation and gives a compact file that loads quickly, but everything since the last snapshot is lost on a crash. The fork() pause matters for latency-sensitive services with large datasets.

AOF records each write, so the loss window shrinks to the fsync interval. The default of once per second bounds loss to about a second; fsync on every write makes each write wait for the disk, which removes most of Redis's speed advantage. Combining RDB and AOF gets a compact restart point plus a small loss window.

For a pure cache, persistence is often turned off entirely: the source of truth has the data, and a restart simply starts cold. Where restarts must not start cold, the chapter points to other mitigations like warm restarts, peer warmup and cross-region replication. And persistence on a single node does not fix the asynchronous replication loss during failover.

quiz.q: What is the durability trade-off between RDB snapshots and AOF with fsync every second?
quiz.a: RDB is compact and quick to restart but can lose minutes of writes; AOF with fsync each second logs every write and loses only about one second.

title: Common mistake: 'persistence is on, so Redis is durable'
body: A common mistake is treating Redis as a durable database because persistence is turned on. Persistence does not close the gaps: replication is asynchronous, and the default AOF setting fsyncs only every second, so a failover can lose recent acknowledged writes. Use Redis as a primary store only for data you can lose or rebuild, such as rate limiter counts, leaderboards you can recompute or sessions users can recreate. Otherwise use a managed variant with a durable log, and read the fine print.
deeper:
The mistake comes from conflating two different durability questions. Persistence answers: if this node restarts, how much of its data comes back? Replication answers: if this node dies, does another node have everything it acknowledged? Redis persistence handles the first partially and does not address the second at all. A write acknowledged by a primary that fails before replicating it is lost regardless of the primary's AOF, because the replica that gets promoted never saw it.

This matters because Redis is so convenient as a primary store for small data. It is fine when losing a second or two of writes, or rebuilding the data, is acceptable. It is dangerous for data of record: account balances, orders, or anything a user expects to survive once confirmed.

The key takeaways restate it: Redis/Valkey Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots and asynchronous replication, and persistence does not make it a strongly durable database. Managed variants with a durable log can change the picture, but only if their guarantees are verified.

quiz.q: Why doesn't turning on persistence make Redis a strongly durable database?
quiz.a: Replication is asynchronous and AOF defaults to fsync every second, so a failover or crash can still lose recently acknowledged writes.

title: The CDN: the biggest cache sits next to the user
body: For large blobs like images, video and JavaScript, the biggest cache is not near the database but near the user. A content delivery network (CDN) is a set of cache servers in many cities and inside internet providers. Akamai and Cloudflare sell this as a service, while Meta runs its own edge caches. Meta's CDN caches serve 70 percent of web requests and cut latency by an order of magnitude, according to the CacheLib paper (2020).
deeper:
A CDN is the outermost caching tier. Where database caches save CPU and database load, a CDN mainly saves distance and bandwidth: a user fetching an image from a server in their own city, or even inside their own internet provider's network, gets it far faster than from a distant data center, and the long-haul network carries far less traffic.

This is where the book's blob storage chapters meet this chapter's caches. The origin, an object store, holds everything durably. The CDN serves the popular part near users. It is the same source-of-truth-plus-disposable-copy relationship as a database and memcache, just at a different layer.

Meta's CDN edge caches are among the systems built on CacheLib, which is why the CacheLib paper reports their numbers. And the CDN workload was one of those it measured as having less skew than textbook Zipf, around alpha 0.55, with popularity changing over hours, pushing toward larger caches that include flash.

quiz.q: How does a CDN relate to blob storage and the idea of a cache?
quiz.a: The object store is the origin and source of truth holding everything; the CDN is a disposable copy of the popular part, served from servers near users.

title: Netflix Open Connect: fill the cache before anyone asks
body: Netflix built its own CDN, Open Connect. It places Open Connect Appliances in its own 60+ data centers and, for free, inside more than a thousand partner ISPs. Because Netflix knows in advance what people are likely to watch, it fills these appliances with content during off-peak hours, called nightly fills. This is proactive caching: the cache is filled before any request arrives, which is only possible when the catalog is known and changes slowly.
deeper:
Most caches in this chapter are demand-filled: data enters the cache when someone misses on it. Open Connect inverts that. The catalog is finite and known, and viewing patterns are predictable enough to decide ahead of time which titles each location will need. Loading them overnight uses network capacity when it is otherwise idle and means peak-hour viewing is served almost entirely from nearby appliances.

Placing appliances inside ISPs for free benefits both sides: the ISP carries less traffic across its external links, and Netflix gets its content as close to viewers as possible.

The chapter is explicit about when this works: only when the catalog is known and changes slowly. A social feed, where new posts appear every second and popularity shifts within hours, cannot be filled ahead of time in the same way. Proactive filling also shares a theme with Netflix's EVCache cross-region replication: in both cases Netflix deliberately fills caches before traffic needs them, so the cache is warm at the critical moment.

quiz.q: Why can Netflix fill Open Connect appliances before anyone requests the content, when most caches can't?
quiz.a: Its catalog is known and changes slowly, and viewing is predictable, so it can load likely titles during off-peak nightly fills. Fast-changing data can't be pre-filled.

title: Miss rate, not hit rate: 99% to 95% means 5x DB load
body: Database load equals read rate times one minus the hit ratio, so the miss rate is what matters. Using illustrative numbers: peak of 2 million profile reads per second, with a database tier that safely handles 100,000. At 99 percent hit ratio, 20,000 reads per second reach the database. At 98 percent, 40,000, double. At 95 percent, 100,000, five times the load and at the limit. At 90 percent, 200,000, ten times: overload. A small-sounding drop is a database outage.
deeper:
The intuition trap is that 99 and 95 sound almost the same. Flip it to misses: 1 percent versus 5 percent is a factor of five. That is why a cache with a 99 percent hit rate is load-bearing: a partial failure that drops it to 95 percent is a database outage in this example.

The chapter's quiz makes the same point with a smaller drop: a hit ratio falling from 99 to 97 percent after a deploy means misses go from 1 percent to 3 percent of reads, so database read load triples.

The same math drives the value of improvements. Every 1 percent of hit ratio gained removes 20,000 database reads per second at peak in this example. That is what justifies spending on larger caches, flash tiers and warmup machinery.

It also explains the failure cascade diagram: cache nodes restart or fail, the hit ratio drops from say 99 to 90, database load rises 10 times, latency and timeouts rise, clients retry, and more load follows. Every mitigation in the chapter attacks one link in that chain.

quiz.q: Your cache hit ratio drops from 99 to 97 percent after a deploy. By how much does database read load change?
quiz.a: It triples: misses go from 1 percent to 3 percent of reads.

title: Sizing a cache: memory says 11 servers, throughput says 15/zone
body: Size a cache by both memory and throughput, and take the larger. Illustrative example: 200 million daily active users, each cached profile about 1 KB plus 100 bytes of overhead. The hot set is about 220 GB; one copy per zone in three zones is about 660 GB, roughly 11 servers with 64 GB usable each. But if one server handles 200,000 gets per second, 2 million reads per second per zone copy needs at least 10 servers per zone, perhaps 15 with failure headroom.
deeper:
Walk through the memory side: 200 million users times 1.1 KB is about 220 GB for one copy. The per-zone replication, as in EVCache, triples it to about 660 GB. Dividing by 64 GB usable per server gives about 11 servers' worth of memory in total.

Now throughput: each zone's copy must serve that zone's reads, and the example assumes 2 million reads per second per zone copy. At 200,000 gets per second per server, that is 10 servers per zone minimum. Adding headroom so the cache survives server failures without a hit-ratio collapse brings it to perhaps 15 per zone.

In this example the two methods give similar answers; the chapter's rule is that when they differ, you size for the larger. A memory-only estimate can badly undersize a high-QPS cache of small items, and a throughput-only estimate can undersize a cache of large items. The 100 bytes per item of overhead is worth noting too: at about 10 percent of each profile, it is the kind of per-object cost Twitter's senior lens warns about.

quiz.q: When memory-based and throughput-based cache sizing give different server counts, which should you use and why?
quiz.a: The larger one: the cache must both hold the hot set and serve the peak request rate with failure headroom, and falling short on either hurts hit ratio or latency.

title: Is flash worth it? Each 1% of hit ratio = 20,000 DB reads/sec
body: In the running example, the full profile set is 1 billion users times 1.1 KB, about 1.1 TB. That is too much for DRAM economically, but it could fit in a few flash-backed servers. Then the long tail of rarely active users, beyond the 200 million daily actives, can hit flash instead of the database. The payoff is concrete: every 1 percent of hit ratio gained removes 20,000 database reads per second at peak in this example.
deeper:
This ties the sizing math to the CacheLib section. A DRAM cache holds the daily-active hot set of about 220 GB per copy. Requests for the other 800 million users' profiles miss and go to the database. Those users are individually rare but collectively significant, exactly the long tail that the CacheLib paper found in real workloads with less skewed popularity than textbook Zipf.

Flash changes the cost of holding that tail: it offers many times more capacity per dollar than DRAM with sub-millisecond reads. Holding all 1.1 TB on a few flash-backed servers converts tail misses into flash hits.

Because database load equals read rate times one minus hit ratio, the gain is large in absolute terms: each percent of hit ratio is 20,000 reads per second at a 2 million read peak, and the database's safe limit in the example is 100,000. The costs to weigh are flash endurance, managed with admission policies, and slightly higher latency for flash hits compared with DRAM.

quiz.q: In the running example, why can a flash tier meaningfully reduce database load even though daily actives already fit in DRAM?
quiz.a: The rarely active long tail misses a DRAM cache; holding the full 1.1 TB on flash turns those misses into hits, and each 1 percent of hit ratio saves 20,000 DB reads/sec.

title: Cold caches: restarting many nodes at once floods the DB
body: A restarted memcached node comes back empty. Restart many at once, for example during a fleet-wide deploy, and the database sees a surge of misses it may not survive. This is the cold cache failure mode. Mitigations from across the chapter: roll restarts slowly so only a small fraction of the cache is cold at a time, use warm restarts (CacheLib), warm a new cluster from a warm peer (Meta's Cold Cluster Warmup), and replicate across regions (EVCache, CacheFront).
deeper:
The hit-ratio math shows why cold caches are dangerous. If the cache normally runs at 99 percent and a deploy empties a tenth of it, the effective hit ratio can drop toward 90 percent, a tenfold increase in database load in the chapter's example, far past its limit.

Each mitigation attacks a different cause. Slow rolling restarts limit how much of the cache is cold at any moment, trading deploy speed for safety. Warm restarts avoid emptying the cache at all by saving and reattaching state. Cold Cluster Warmup handles brand-new clusters by reading misses from a warm peer, bringing capacity up in hours instead of days. Cross-region replication handles the largest case: a whole region's traffic moving elsewhere.

Because production caches restart frequently, with many production caches running less than 7 days between restarts, this is not a rare event. It is a routine operation that must be designed so it never looks like an outage to the database.

quiz.q: Why is restarting many cache nodes at once dangerous, and name two mitigations?
quiz.a: Restarted nodes are empty, so hit ratio drops and misses surge onto the database. Mitigations: slow rolling restarts, warm restarts, warm-peer cluster warmup, cross-region replication.

title: DynamoDB's trick: keep the backend busy even on cache hits
body: The DynamoDB paper warns not to let caches hide work the system must be able to do without them. DynamoDB's request routers cache partition metadata locally, but even on a cache hit they send an asynchronous refresh call to the MemDS metadata fleet. So MemDS always serves a constant volume of traffic regardless of hit ratio. This costs extra load in normal times, but prevents cascading failures when caches become ineffective, because MemDS was never sized for a hit ratio.
deeper:
This is the cache as hidden capacity dependency failure mode, and DynamoDB's answer is unusual: deliberately give up the offload benefit to keep the backend honest. Normally a high hit ratio lets the backend fleet shrink. Then, if caches suddenly become ineffective, say after a mass restart or a change in access pattern, the backend sees a load spike it was never provisioned for, and fails. Because the routers' refresh calls go out whether or not they hit, MemDS load never depends on the hit ratio, so there is no spike to survive.

The general guidance from the chapter: keep the database able to survive a realistic miss storm, or add admission control and load shedding in front of it so overload is refused gracefully rather than cascading.

This connects back to the opening senior staff lens: if the cache were empty right now, could the database survive? DynamoDB engineered the metadata path so the answer is always yes, at the cost of constant extra work.

quiz.q: Why do DynamoDB's request routers send refresh calls to MemDS even on cache hits?
quiz.a: So MemDS serves constant traffic regardless of hit ratio and is always sized for it; if caches become ineffective, there is no sudden load spike to cause cascading failures.

title: Failure rehashing: one dead node, then the next, then the next
body: When a cache node dies in a consistent-hashing cluster, its keys are typically rehashed onto the surviving nodes. That sounds harmless, but load per key is uneven. If the dead node held a hot key, the node inheriting it receives a sudden surge on top of its own load, may be overloaded and die, and its keys move on to the next node, which dies in turn. One failure cascades through the cluster. Meta's Gutter pool avoids this.
deeper:
The root cause is that rehashing assumes keys are interchangeable units of load, and they are not. Meta observed that a single key can account for 20 percent of a server's requests. Moving that key to a neighbor that was already running near normal capacity can push it over.

Meta's Gutter pool breaks the chain: about 1 percent of servers kept idle absorb a failed server's traffic, so no healthy server's load changes. Gutter entries expire quickly to limit staleness. It cut client-visible failures by 99 percent.

The chapter's quiz answer summarizes: load per key is uneven, a hot key moved to a healthy node can overload it and cause cascading failures, and Meta sends failed nodes' traffic to a small, idle Gutter pool with short TTLs. Replicating hot keys, via replicated pools or per-zone copies as in EVCache, also reduces the risk, since losing one copy leaves others serving the key.

quiz.q: Why is rehashing a failed cache node's keys onto surviving nodes risky?
quiz.a: Load per key is uneven; a hot key moved onto a healthy node can overload it, which fails and pushes load onward, cascading through the cluster.

title: Retry storms: when timeouts multiply the load
body: Retry storms happen when clients retry cache timeouts by going to the database, or retry database timeouts repeatedly. Each retry adds load exactly when the system is already struggling, so the load grows as things get worse. The chapter's guidance: cap retries, use backoff, and treat cache errors as misses only when the database can take the extra load. Meta's clients, for example, skip the cache fill after a UDP get error, to avoid adding load.
deeper:
Retries are the last link in the chapter's failure cascade: cache nodes restart or fail, the hit ratio drops, database load rises, database latency and timeouts rise, and clients retry, which pushes database load higher still. Without limits, this loop can keep a database overloaded even after the original trigger is gone.

Capping retries bounds how much any one request can amplify load. Backoff spreads retries out in time so they do not arrive as a synchronized wave. Treating cache errors as misses is the default look-aside behavior, but it quietly converts every cache problem into database load, so it is only safe when the database has headroom.

Meta's choice to skip the fill after a UDP get error is a small example of load-aware design: the client still fetches the value, but does not add a set to a cache that might be congested. The diagram's other mitigations for the database stage, leases, request coalescing and load shedding, also help by reducing duplicate queries and refusing excess work gracefully.

quiz.q: Why should clients cap retries and use backoff when cache or database requests time out?
quiz.a: Retries add load precisely when the system is overloaded, amplifying the problem; caps limit amplification and backoff spreads retries out.

title: Stale data that never expires
body: One failure mode is almost embarrassingly simple: a missed invalidation with no TTL lives forever. Whether the delete was lost to an app crash, dropped by the network, or undone by a stale set, the wrong value stays in the cache indefinitely if nothing forces it out. Users see old data with no end in sight, and the bug can be very hard to trace. The rule the chapter repeats is always set a TTL.
deeper:
Why does this happen in practice? Teams often skip TTLs because they already invalidate on write and a TTL seems redundant, or because they want the highest possible hit ratio. But the invalidation section showed at least three ways invalidation can fail: stale sets, replication-lag refills and lost invalidations. Even commit-log invalidators like McSqueal and Flux can miss a key through a bug in key extraction or a write path that bypasses them.

A TTL does not prevent any of these, but it caps the damage. A stale entry becomes a stale entry for at most the TTL rather than forever. That turns a potentially permanent data bug into a transient one.

The cost of adding a TTL is some extra misses as entries expire, which should be spread with jitter so many keys do not expire together, and handled with leases, coalescing or early refresh for hot keys. That is a small price compared with data that never corrects itself.

quiz.q: Why is a missing TTL dangerous even when you invalidate caches on every write?
quiz.a: Invalidations can fail through lost deletes, stale sets or replica refills; without a TTL, any such stale entry stays wrong forever.

title: Fan-out: a 500-key page waits for its slowest key
body: Large values and high fan-out are another failure mode. A page that fetches 500 keys from the cache must wait for the slowest of those 500 responses before it can render. The more keys a request touches, the more likely it is to hit at least one slow server, so page latency is governed by the tail, not the average. Many large responses arriving at once also cause incast congestion. The fix: batch requests, cap fan-out, and watch incast.
deeper:
Fan-out turns rare slowness into common slowness. If each cache read has only a small chance of being slow, a request reading hundreds of keys is still quite likely to include at least one slow one. Meta's memcache design grapples with this directly: a page load can fetch hundreds of keys, so latency depends on fan-out.

Large values add to the problem. Each large response takes longer to transfer and fills network buffers faster, so many arriving together at one web server can overflow switch buffers, the incast congestion Meta handles with a sliding window of outstanding requests.

The mitigations are structural. Batch many keys per request to the same server to reduce round trips. Cap fan-out by designing pages and data models that need fewer keys, or by grouping related data so it can be fetched together, for example with Redis hash tags that place related keys in one slot. And monitor for incast, since it shows up as packet loss and latency spikes rather than obvious errors.

quiz.q: Why does fetching 500 cache keys for one page hurt latency more than the average per-key latency suggests?
quiz.a: The page waits for the slowest of 500 responses, so tail latency dominates; many simultaneous responses can also cause incast congestion.

title: Eviction surprises: a new feature evicts your valuable keys
body: Eviction surprises happen when a new feature starts writing many low-value keys into a shared cache. The cache fills, its eviction policy pushes out older entries, and some of those were valuable, frequently read keys serving another workload. That workload's hit ratio falls and its database load rises, even though nobody changed its code. The fix is isolation: use separate pools, as Meta does, or separate clusters per workload, so one workload's churn cannot destroy another's cache.
deeper:
The danger is that the damage shows up far from the cause. The team shipping the new feature sees nothing wrong; the team whose database suddenly runs hot sees no change in their own code. Because a small hit-ratio drop multiplies database load, a feature that evicts even a few percent of another workload's hot set can cause real trouble. In the chapter's example, dropping from 99 to 95 percent is five times the database load.

Meta's pools give each workload its own servers and memory, and mcrouter routes keys to the right pool by key prefix, so a low-value, high-churn key set cannot evict valuable keys elsewhere. Separate clusters per workload achieve the same isolation at a coarser level.

Isolation also helps with sizing: each pool can be sized by its own memory and throughput needs. Twitter's slab calcification problem is a related memory-allocation surprise inside a single cache, solved by Twemcache's slab-level eviction.

quiz.q: How can launching a new feature raise database load for an unrelated service, and what prevents it?
quiz.a: Its low-value keys fill a shared cache and evict the other service's valuable keys, lowering its hit ratio. Separate pools or clusters per workload prevent this.

title: The failure cascade: from a few restarts to a DB meltdown
body: Cache failures cascade in a predictable chain. Cache nodes restart or fail. The hit ratio drops, for example from 99 to 90 percent. Database load rises tenfold. Database latency and timeouts rise. Clients retry, adding still more load. Each link can be broken. The Gutter pool, warm restarts and cold cluster warmup keep the hit ratio from dropping. Leases, request coalescing and load shedding protect the database once load rises, while capped retries with backoff stop the retry loop.
deeper:
Seen as a whole, almost every technique in the chapter maps to a stage of this cascade.

Stage one, cache capacity lost: Meta's Gutter pool absorbs failed servers' traffic, CacheLib warm restarts keep deployed nodes full, Cold Cluster Warmup fills new clusters from warm peers, slow rolling restarts limit how much is cold at once, and cross-region replication (EVCache, CacheFront) keeps failover regions warm.

Stage two, database load surges: leases limit refills to one client per key, cutting Meta's herd-prone peak from 17,000 to 1,300 queries per second; request coalescing merges duplicate misses; load shedding and admission control refuse excess work gracefully; serving stale on error avoids hitting the database at all.

Stage three, retries: cap them, add backoff, and treat cache errors as misses only when the database can take it.

The design-time version is the opening senior lens: could the database survive if this cache were empty? DynamoDB's constant-work refresh to MemDS is the extreme answer: make the backend's load independent of hit ratio.

quiz.q: In the cache failure cascade, which mitigations act before database load rises and which act after?
quiz.a: Before: Gutter pool, warm restarts, cold cluster warmup keep hit ratio up. After: leases, request coalescing and load shedding protect the database, plus capped retries with backoff.
